evidence.text: Based on the three necessary conditions that I derived from the review (agency, surprise, and value), I define serendipity as ‘surprising discovery that results from unplanned moments in which our decisions and actions lead to valuable outcomes’.
In a recent review, Busch (2024) identified three necessary conditions that distinguish serendipity from related concepts.

In contrast to pure luck, Busch (2024) argues that in addition to the necessary conditions of surprise and value forming luck, respectively, agency is a third necessary condition for serendipity to happen.
Serendipity involves the convergence of agency, surprise, and value ( Busch, 2024 ), and implies purposeful action in response to unforeseen cues ( Busch and Barkema, 2022 ; Rauch and Ansari, 2022 ).
Value, together with agency and surprise, is one of the necessary conditions of serendipity (Busch, 2024).
Recent work frames serendipity as the interplay of unexpectedness, agency, and value ( Busch, 2024 ; Busch and Grimes, 2023 ).
In essence, serendipity involves the interaction of three elements: a resource (sagacity), an event (contingencies), and an activity (the individual is already on a journey).
Serendipity is conceptualized as the combination of search (directed effort), contingency (favourable accidents), and prior knowledge (sagacity).

Because serendipity is characterized by “some combination of search (directed effort), contingency (favorable accidents) and prior knowledge (sagacity) ” (Dew, 2009 : 736), attracting stakeholders' pre-commitments and enlarging the means available to the venture serves to enhance the pool of knowledge required to detect and act on key contingencies.

Dew (2009, p. 739) suggests that serendipity “involves the interaction of three elements (i) a resource (sagacity), (ii) an event (contingency), (iii) an activity (the individual is already on a journey).
Entrepreneurial serendipity also contains the three elements of serendipity from Dew’s (2009) conceptual model: knowledge, search and contingency.

Defined in the management literature as a “ search leading to unintended discovery ” ( Dew, 2009 , p. 735), serendipity is more than mere chance, arising from the interplay of searching, contingency, and prior knowledge ( Dew, 2009 ).

Horace Walpole, who coined the word, said in a letter of Jan. 28, 1754, that he took it from the title of a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip; the princes “were always making discoveries by accident and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of.”

Chute calls sortes Walpolianae,” for, whether sortes is translated as “luck” or “fate,” it lacks the mixture of those two ingredients that Walpole irrevocably included in the complex meaning of serendipity: accident and sagacity.
We define serendipity as entrepreneurs “making discoveries, by accidents and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of” (Merton & Barber, 2004, p. 2).

In his letter to his diplomatist friend Walpole mentioned a special type of luck that these princes bestow: he termed it serendipity, after the ancient tale, which resulted from the combination of an accident with sagacity or perspicacity in understanding.
Serendipity in finding and exploring new things is, however, believed to be a result of “accident and sagacity”, rather than accident or luck alone ( Friedel, 2001 ).

Referencing the Persian fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip, Horace Walpole described serendipity as “making discoveries, by accident and sagacity, of things they were not in quest of” (quoted in Merton and Barber, 2004).
He refers to serendipity as an unexpected discovery found from the combination of accident and sagacity ( Rosenman, 2001 ).
Columbus’ discovery of the ‘New World’ was, of course, an example of serendipity: of making a discovery, by accident and sagacity, of things not in quest of.

codes.label: Finding something not sought
codes.definition: Serendipity means finding something one was not looking for, often while pursuing a different aim. Finding what one set out to find does not count. Authors leave open whether the find only needs to be unsought at that moment or must also have been unknown and unsuspected.
codes.applies_when: The person describes coming upon an idea, contact, resource or opportunity different from what they were seeking at the time.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person found exactly what they were searching for. Also distinguish from 'Discovery solves a different problem': use that code when the account stresses that the find answered a different problem or question than the one pursued.

codes.label: Discovery solves a different problem
codes.definition: While seeking a solution to one problem, the person notices something that solves a different problem, or answers a question nobody had yet asked. The accident lies in how the discovery relates to the original question.
codes.applies_when: The person was pursuing one goal or question and the result addressed a different need or answered a question they had not set out to ask.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Finding something not sought' when the account only says the find was unsought, without linking it to a different problem or question.

codes.label: Need and solution found together
codes.definition: A need and its solution are discovered at the same moment as a pair. The problem is recognised only afterwards, if at all, by comparing the new arrangement with the old one.
codes.applies_when: The person says they were not aware of a problem or need until they came across the solution, for example 'I didn't think we had a problem, but now I see we do'.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Discovery solves a different problem' when the person already had a defined problem and the find solved another one.

codes.label: Searching for something specific
codes.definition: When the unexpected event happened, the founder was already looking for something: an idea, a solution, customers or a way forward. Needed for the narrow verdict (Dew 2009).
codes.applies_when: The founder was working on a specific problem, product or goal at the time. For example: 'I'd been trying ideas for months when...'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder was not looking for anything at the time. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Version 1.0 (25 Oct 2026): one answer of the search-state question (level 1).

draft_wording.label: Search leading to unintended discovery
draft_wording.definition: Serendipity is an active search that ends in an unintended discovery. It needs three things together: ongoing search or effort, a chance event, and prior knowledge that reveals the event's significance. Without the search element the episode is chance or luck. This view conflicts with authors who see opportunity discovery as happening without search.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person was actively working on or looking for something and, in the course of it, came across something valuable they were not looking for, drawing on what they already knew.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Discovery without search' when the person stresses they were not searching at all. Do not apply when the person found the intended target of the search.

codes.label: Discovery without search
codes.definition: Opportunities come to people who were not searching for them. Discovery is recognising the value of information received by other means, because an opportunity cannot be searched for until it is known.
codes.applies_when: The founder stresses that they were not looking for a business idea or opportunity when they came across it and recognised it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Search leading to unintended discovery' when the person was actively searching for something else and found the opportunity along the way.

codes.label: Agency: acted on it
codes.definition: The founder did something with the unexpected event: followed it up, tried it, or built on it. Without this, it is luck, not serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes their own response to the event and links the result to it. For example: 'I wrote back that night and offered to build it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The benefit arrived with no action by the founder. Use "Pure luck, no action".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Agency: one of Busch's three conditions; decides the broad verdict. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Agency: the founder acted on it'

draft_wording.label: Acting on the unexpected
draft_wording.definition: Serendipity requires agency: the person acts on, seizes or exploits an unplanned event through purposeful action. This agency separates serendipity from pure luck, which simply befalls a person.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes doing something with an unexpected event, such as following it up, framing it as an opportunity or exploiting it, and links the good outcome to that action or effort.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Accident plus sagacity' when the account centres on recognising or interpreting the event rather than acting on it. Do not apply when the benefit arrived with no action by the person.

codes.label: Serendipity as a capability
codes.definition: Serendipity is a capability or faculty for recognising and extracting value from unexpected occurrences, not merely the occurrence itself. Merton argues it is both a personal faculty and an event, and coders can note which framing is used.
codes.applies_when: The account presents serendipity as an ability or trait of the person or firm, for example a knack for spotting and absorbing outside knowledge or for turning chance to advantage.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Acting on the unexpected' when the account describes a specific action in a specific episode rather than a general ability.

codes.label: Surprise
codes.definition: Something happened that the founder did not expect, plan or intend.
codes.applies_when: The founder says an event, contact, result or reaction was unexpected or not part of the plan. For example: 'I never expected anyone to ask for that.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder got what they planned and expected, on schedule. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Surprise: one of Busch's three conditions; decides the broad verdict. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The founder got what they planned and expected. A goal reached on schedule is not a surprise.'

draft_wording.definition: Serendipity rests on something unexpected, unplanned or not intended. The outcome falls outside what the person foresaw. Surprise opens further exploration rather than closing a problem.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes an event, piece of information or result as unexpected, surprising or outside what they had planned or predicted.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Anomaly against expectations' when the account stresses that the event contradicted the person's knowledge or theories, not merely that it was unforeseen.

codes.label: Anomaly against expectations
codes.definition: The serendipitous datum is anomalous: it contrasts with prior experience or expectations and becomes strategic by setting a new direction. Without such contrast an event is mere chance.
codes.applies_when: The person notes that what they encountered was odd or contradicted what they knew or predicted, and that they then built on it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Surprise' when the event was only unexpected in occurrence and still fit the person's existing understanding.

codes.label: Realising what was overlooked
codes.definition: Genuine discovery comes with the surprise of realising one had overlooked something readily available ('it was under my nose'). It reduces ignorance the person did not know they had.
codes.applies_when: The person describes a sudden realisation that an opportunity or fact had been in front of them all along.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Surprise' when the unexpectedness concerns a new event rather than something already present that had gone unnoticed.

codes.label: Chance trigger
codes.definition: The trigger is a chance event that happened without design, with no obvious cause or link to a present need. It is one of many possible triggers of action and is not a necessary precondition.
codes.applies_when: The person describes an unplanned, coincidental or accidental event whose cause they cannot identify or that arose independently of their plans, and which set things in motion.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Surprise' when the account is about the person's sense of unexpectedness rather than the accidental origin of the event.

codes.label: Value
codes.definition: The unexpected event led to something the founder sees as worth having: an idea, customer, product, partner or turning point.
codes.applies_when: The founder presents what followed as useful or important for them or the venture. For example: 'That one email became our biggest customer.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: Nothing of value came of it. Use "Nothing came of it".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Value: one of Busch's three conditions; decides the broad verdict. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'Nothing of value came of it; code outcome-25 (nothing came of it) and leave this code off.'

draft_wording.label: Beneficial outcome
draft_wording.definition: Serendipity is a happy accident: the unexpected discovery yields something valuable, such as an opportunity, windfall or turning point. One source deliberately drops this requirement and counts unplanned findings of little value as serendipitous.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account presents an unplanned discovery, encounter or turn of events as useful, beneficial or contributing to the venture's success.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Value judged by the finder, often in hindsight' when the account stresses that the value was personal, potential or recognised only later.

codes.label: Value judged by the finder, often in hindsight
codes.definition: Whether something was unexpected and valuable is judged from the individual's viewpoint. Value is potential and must be realised, and events are often labelled serendipitous only in hindsight. An event can be deliberate for one party yet unplanned for another.
codes.applies_when: The person values a find that others overlooked, says its usefulness had to be realised through further action, labels events serendipitous only after they turned out well, or notes that someone else acted deliberately while the event was unplanned for them.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Beneficial outcome' when the account simply states that the outcome was valuable, without the personal or retrospective framing.

codes.label: Serendipity as a process
codes.definition: Serendipity is a process and its outcome, not a single event. It runs from a trigger, through a connection to something relevant, to acting on that connection, and often unfolds through effort, alertness and testing over time and across people. This contrasts with authors who treat breakthroughs as fleeting moments.
codes.applies_when: The account traces a sequence from an unexpected moment, through linking it to a goal or need, to follow-up action, or describes the discovery as building gradually.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Unpredictable opportune moment' when the account presents the breakthrough as a sudden, fleeting moment rather than an unfolding sequence.

codes.label: Connecting separate elements
codes.definition: Serendipity involves combining two or more observations, events or pieces of information into a meaningful new pairing that is then put to use. This includes recognising that something that first seemed out of place is useful.
codes.applies_when: The person describes linking an unexpected observation or piece of information with something else they knew, so that the pieces 'add up' into a new idea or opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Serendipity as a process' when the account traces the whole sequence through to action, rather than centring on the act of combining elements.

codes.label: Existing thing finds an unintended use
codes.definition: Something that already exists, such as a product, skill, knowledge, technology or earlier decision, turns out by chance to serve a purpose nobody intended, often with little adjustment and without foresight.
codes.applies_when: The account describes capabilities, assets or decisions developed for one purpose that later proved useful for a new venture, market or problem nobody had anticipated.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Finding something not sought' when the find is new information or an opportunity encountered, rather than a new use for something the person already had.

codes.label: Unpredictable opportune moment
codes.definition: Serendipitous moments cannot be predicted, scheduled or willed. They are opportune times when 'the time is right', or fleeting coincidences, though they may rest on prior engagement with the field.
codes.applies_when: The person describes a breakthrough or lucky break that came at an unscheduled, favourable moment or from a passing coincidence they could not have planned.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Serendipity as a process' when the account stresses gradual unfolding through effort over time.

codes.label: Unplanned encounter with new people
codes.definition: A chance encounter exposes the person to people they would not otherwise have met and to unfamiliar information. The connection happens spontaneously, not through a deliberate attempt to bring people together.
codes.applies_when: The person describes meeting someone by chance, or a connection arising spontaneously, often after direct efforts had failed, and this interaction shaped the venture idea.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance trigger' when the unplanned event does not involve meeting people. Do not apply when the meeting was a deliberately targeted contact.

codes.label: Unexpected in time or place
codes.definition: The unexpectedness may lie in when a find occurs or in where it is found ('where one least expects it'), rather than in what is found.
codes.applies_when: The account stresses that a find came at an unexpected moment or in an unexpected setting.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Finding something not sought' when what was found differed from what was sought, rather than only its timing or location.

codes.label: Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly
codes.definition: The founder was looking for something specific and found it, but through chance: an unexpected source, path or moment. The goal stayed the same.
codes.applies_when: A known problem or need was solved by something that turned up unexpectedly. For example: 'We needed a supplier, and the guy next to me on the plane ran one.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The find answered a different problem or changed the goal. Use "Walpolian: sought one, found another".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Common founder pattern; widely supported (17 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code. Named after Yaqub's (2018) Mertonian type; the type group follows Yaqub's typology | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Found what they sought, by an unexpected route (Mertonian)'

draft_wording.label: Sought goal reached by an unexpected route
draft_wording.definition: The person was already looking for a solution, item or goal of a known kind and got it, but through a chance source, route or timing. Authors called it Archimedes, Mertonian or Archimedean serendipity treat it as a full type. Authors who call it pseudo-serendipity say it is not true serendipity because the goal does not change.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person had a defined problem or wanted something specific, and the answer or item turned up from an unrelated source, a coincidence, an unusual path or at a lucky moment. The original goal stays the same, or the problem is only reframed.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The chance find answered a different or previously unrecognised problem, or redirected the goal. Use 'Looking for one thing, finding another' for that.

codes.label: Walpolian: sought one, found another
codes.definition: While working on one goal, the founder found something valuable for a different purpose, and turned toward it.
codes.applies_when: A project or search ended up producing a different product, market or direction. For example: 'We were building a tool for agencies and schools started buying it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The original goal was met, but in an unexpected way. Use "Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly".
There was no search at all. Use "Not looking at all".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Classic pattern; widely supported (12 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code. Named after Yaqub's (2018) Walpolian type; the type group follows Yaqub's typology | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Looked for one thing, found another (Walpolian)'; Not when was: 'The original goal was met by an unexpected route (type-01), or there was no search at all (type-03).'

draft_wording.label: Looking for one thing, finding another
draft_wording.definition: While actively pursuing one problem or goal, the person stumbles on something of value that answers a different or previously unrecognised problem, often changing their objective. Authors call this Walpolian, Post-it, Columbian or true serendipity. Merton notes that this 'by-product of search' sense came later than Walpole's own usage.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account shows a targeted search or project that ended up yielding a different product, use, market or direction, and the person turned aside from the original aim to pursue it.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The find solved the original problem by an unexpected route (use 'Sought goal reached by an unexpected route'), or there was no search at all (use 'Unsought opportunity with no search under way').

codes.label: Not looking at all
codes.definition: The founder was not looking for a business or an idea. A need and a way to meet it turned up together in everyday life, and they saw an opportunity.
codes.applies_when: The founder was not looking for a business or a solution when it happened. For example: 'I made it for myself, then people kept asking for one.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder already wanted to start some business. Use "Open to any business".
The founder was after a specific goal. Use "Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly" or "Walpolian: sought one, found another".
codes.reason: Version 1.0 (25 Oct 2026): one answer of the search-state question (level 1).

draft_wording.label: Unsought opportunity with no search under way
draft_wording.definition: The person was not looking for anything in particular, and often had no intention of starting a business. They unexpectedly came upon a need and a way to meet it together, and recognised it as an opportunity. Authors call this thunderbolt, Galilean or spontaneous recognition, or discovery from complete ignorance.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes coming upon a business idea, offer or gap during everyday life or ordinary operations, without searching. This includes stumbling into a venture by solving a need for themselves or others before any decision to become an entrepreneur.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The person already wanted to start some business and was open to any opportunity (use 'Open search for any opportunity'). Also excluded: exploration that met a need already known (use 'Untargeted exploration meets an existing need').

codes.label: Open to any business
codes.definition: The founder wanted to start or grow a business but had no specific idea, and a suitable opportunity came along by chance (Mirvahedi and Morrish's 'entrepreneurial serendipity').
codes.applies_when: The founder wanted to start something but had no specific idea in mind. For example: 'I knew I wanted to work for myself; then a friend mentioned...'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder had no wish to start a business. Use "Not looking at all".
The founder was already pursuing a specific idea. Use "Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly" or "Walpolian: sought one, found another".
codes.reason: Version 1.0 (25 Oct 2026): one answer of the search-state question (level 1).

draft_wording.label: Open search for any opportunity
draft_wording.definition: The person is looking for some unspecified opportunity, such as wanting to be self-employed or to expand, without a particular idea. Chance circumstances then bring a suitable opportunity, which a prepared mind seizes.
draft_wording.applies_when: The founder wanted to run their own business or grow without a set idea, and an opportunity came along by chance that they took up.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The person had no wish or readiness to start a business at all (use 'Unsought opportunity with no search under way').

codes.label: Bushian: exploring, met existing need
codes.definition: The founder was exploring, browsing or tinkering without a specific problem in mind, and came across something that met a need they already had (Yaqub's Bushian type).
codes.applies_when: The founder was trying things out or browsing, and found the answer to a need they already had. For example: 'I was playing with a new tool and realised it fixed our shipping problem.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder was searching for that answer. Use "Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly".
The need only appeared after the find. Use "Stephanian: solution first, problem later".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Yaqub's (2018) Bushian type, so the type group covers his full typology. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Exploring with no problem in mind, solved an existing one (Bushian)'

draft_wording.label: Untargeted exploration meets an existing need
draft_wording.definition: Trying out, experimenting or browsing with no specific problem in mind leads to something that resolves a need or problem the person or firm already had (Bushian serendipity).
draft_wording.applies_when: Play, experimentation or browsing unexpectedly answered a problem that already existed but was not being actively pursued.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The find answers a problem that did not yet exist or was not yet recognised and is only linked later (use 'Solution found before its problem').

codes.label: Stephanian: solution first, problem later
codes.definition: The founder came upon something interesting with no use for it at the time, kept it, and later found the problem or market it solved (Yaqub's Stephanian type).
codes.applies_when: The founder describes a find, skill or product that sat unused until a need turned up. For example: 'We had built that feature years ago; only when customers asked did we see what it was for.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
Problem and solution came together. Use "Not looking at all".
The find met a need that already existed. Use "Bushian: exploring, met existing need".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Yaqub's (2018) Stephanian type, so the type group covers his full typology. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Found the solution first, the problem later (Stephanian)'; Not when was: 'The problem and the solution turned up together (type-03), or the find met a need the founder already had (type-05).'

draft_wording.label: Solution found before its problem
draft_wording.definition: Something is discovered or invented before any problem or market for it is known. It is kept, sometimes without its value being seen, and later linked to a need that emerges (Stephanian serendipity, solution before problem, pre-discovery).
draft_wording.applies_when: The person found or made something with no immediate use, shelved it or kept it in mind, and only later recognised the need, market or commercial potential it served.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The discovery immediately met an already-existing need (use 'Untargeted exploration meets an existing need').

codes.label: Foreground versus background serendipity
codes.definition: Foreground serendipity confirms or advances a person's current focus or direction. Background serendipity triggers a latent interest and may change that direction.
codes.applies_when: The account shows whether the chance find pushed the existing direction forward, or awakened a dormant interest that shifted the person's course.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The coder is only judging whether the find solved the searched-for problem or a different one. Use the search-based types for that; this code concerns fit with existing focus and latent interests.

codes.label: Everyday micro serendipity
codes.definition: Small, frequent chance occurrences, such as a useful piece of information, a minor encounter or an accident with materials. They are noticed and adjust what a person does, with modest benefit. This is the weak end of a weak-to-strong continuum (little-s serendipity).
codes.applies_when: The account describes minor everyday lucky finds or encounters that changed a task or decision but not the person's overall path.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The chance event radically changed the person's career, such as founding an unforeseen venture (use 'Life-changing serendipitous critical event').

codes.label: Life-changing serendipitous critical event
codes.definition: A rare, clearly bounded chance episode that is causally decisive for the outcome and produces radical change, such as creating a venture the person would otherwise not have started. This is the strong end of the continuum (Big-S serendipity).
codes.applies_when: A specific unplanned conversation, request or event is described as what turned the person's professional path toward the venture.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The chance event was small and everyday (use 'Everyday micro serendipity'). Also excluded: a general trigger such as available financing or a poor economy that is not a bounded chance episode.

codes.label: Sudden moment versus unfolding process
codes.definition: Serendipity can be narrated as a single eureka moment or flash of insight, or as an opportunity that unfolds over time through doubt, exploration and reinterpretation.
codes.applies_when: The coder can see whether the person tells the opportunity as one sudden flash or as a drawn-out process.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The issue is the size of the impact rather than its timing (use the micro or critical event codes).

codes.label: Missed serendipity
codes.definition: A surprising fact, contact or opportunity is noticed or is right in front of the person, but is not recognised or not acted on, so its value is lost (negative serendipity).
codes.applies_when: The person describes noticing something unexpected, such as unexpected customer interest, but failing to see its value or to pursue it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person acted on an unexpected bad event and turned it to value (use 'Unfortunate event turned to advantage').

codes.label: Unfortunate event turned to advantage
codes.definition: An unexpected negative event, such as a rejection, setback or resistance, becomes the occasion for finding or pursuing something valuable, rather than a reason to quit.
codes.applies_when: The account describes an unforeseen setback during the venture's development that the founder leveraged into a new direction or gain.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person's own setup repeatedly produced unlucky outcomes (use 'Zemblanity'), or an opportunity was simply missed (use 'Missed serendipity').

codes.label: Prepared or self-made luck
codes.definition: Chance events become fortunate because of the person's or firm's position, preparation, knowledge, alertness, belief and action. Entrepreneurs often hold this view alongside the view that luck simply happened to them.
codes.applies_when: The person says 'you make your own luck', or describes having prepared themselves or the firm in ways that let them recognise and seize an unexpected change.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The gain needed no action or capability (use 'Pure luck'), or the person describes an enduring personal knack for lucky finds (use 'Serendipity as a personal gift').

codes.label: Serendipity as a personal gift
codes.definition: Serendipity understood as an enduring quality, knack or faculty that lets some people repeatedly make happy accidental discoveries. This is set against serendipity as a one-off event or as external luck. Dictionaries and authors are inconsistent on which sense applies.
codes.applies_when: The person describes themselves or someone else as having a recurring knack for stumbling on valuable things, or as always making such discoveries.
codes.does_not_apply_when: A single fortunate occurrence is described, or the find is credited to deliberate preparation and action (use 'Prepared or self-made luck').

codes.label: Engineered serendipity
codes.definition: Conditions for unexpected outcomes are deliberately created, while the specific result or contact stays unplanned. Examples are organised events, designed spaces, or deliberately introduced randomness and crises (artificial serendipity, intentional accident). Topic-focused settings such as conferences also shape what is exchanged.
codes.applies_when: The person describes arranging, or taking part in, a structured setting or deliberate process meant to make something unforeseen turn up, which then produced a useful contact or idea.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The meeting or event simply happened without anyone arranging conditions for it (use 'Chance encounter').

codes.label: Collaborative serendipity
codes.definition: Unexpected synergies discovered when team members or parties juxtapose very different ideas or lines of action in working together.
codes.applies_when: A valuable unforeseen idea emerged from combining different people's contributions within a collaboration.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The discovery depended on information passed along a wider network or built up over a long process involving many actors (use 'Collective serendipity').

codes.label: Collective serendipity
codes.definition: Discovery made possible only by many actors over time: inputs noticed and passed along by others in a network, matched in a chance meeting, or accumulated contributions from many people. It is not one person's moment of insight.
codes.applies_when: Success is described as depending on several people encountering and relaying information, or on many contributions over time, each adding unforeseen pieces.
codes.does_not_apply_when: A small team directly combined their ideas (use 'Collaborative serendipity'), or a single individual encountered and recognised the opportunity.

codes.label: Distributed serendipity
codes.definition: Someone other than the original discoverer finds a new use for a discovery, often after it has been shared. The discoverer may anticipate that others will find such uses.
codes.applies_when: The new use or opportunity was identified by a different person from the one who made the original discovery.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The discoverer alone found the new use (use 'New use for an existing thing').

codes.label: Accidental discovery itself
codes.definition: The chance element is the making of the discovery itself, such as stumbling on a new substance, finding or technology (Type I serendipity).
codes.applies_when: The account describes accidentally discovering or creating something new, such as a material, effect or technology.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The thing already existed and the surprise was a new use for it (use 'New use for an existing thing').

codes.label: New use for an existing thing
codes.definition: Finding an unanticipated function or market for an existing technology, product, skill or resource (exaptation, Type II serendipity). This includes applying a technology in another field or recombining technologies.
codes.applies_when: The person describes discovering that something they already had or knew could serve a surprising new purpose, field or market.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The thing itself was newly discovered by accident (use 'Accidental discovery itself'), or the new use was found by someone else (use 'Distributed serendipity').

codes.label: Repurposing something in use versus something without use
codes.definition: Exaptive sources are of two kinds. 'Franklins' are existing structures already in use that are co-opted for a supplementary use. 'Miltons' are discoveries or things with no current function that later find a use.
codes.applies_when: The account shows either repurposing something already functioning, or finding a use for something that previously had none.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The coder is judging only whether a find awaited a later problem (use 'Solution found before its problem'). This code concerns whether the source already had a function.

codes.label: Added use versus redirected development
codes.definition: A distinction between an established product gaining an additional use (repurposing) and a product still in development being redirected mid-course toward a different use (redevelopment).
codes.applies_when: The account describes either an existing product gaining a new market or use, or a project under development being switched to another application.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The coder is only noting a new use without the established-versus-in-development contrast (use 'New use for an existing thing').

codes.label: New mechanism versus known principle
codes.definition: A distinction between unexpected uses that rest on the same underlying phenomenon, which could in principle be reasoned out by analogy, and uses that rest on a genuinely new, unknown phenomenon. The latter cannot be foreseen and are rarer but more radical.
codes.applies_when: The coder can tell whether the surprising use relied on a known principle or on a newly revealed mechanism.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The issue is whether the find was new to the person or new to the world (use 'New to me versus new to the world').

codes.label: New to me versus new to the world
codes.definition: A chance encounter may lead someone to adopt an existing need-solution pair that is new only to them. It may also spark a need-solution pair that is new to the world, such as an idea transferred to an entirely different situation.
codes.applies_when: The account shows either taking up a solution encountered as it was, or being prompted by an encounter to create something novel for another context.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The distinction concerns the underlying mechanism of an exaptation (use 'New mechanism versus known principle').

codes.label: Random chance versus unintended design consequence
codes.definition: Authors keep apart two triggers. One is an a-causal random event unrelated to any design, such as a contaminant or a lucky office-mate. The other is an unexpected outcome causally produced by a design or testing process, such as side effects or unintended uses.
codes.applies_when: Mark random chance when the trigger was unconnected to the person's plans. Mark unintended consequence when the surprise came from how the person's own product, project or trial was set up.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The distinction is whether the trigger came from the outside world or from the person's own mind (use 'External versus internal chance').

codes.label: External versus internal chance
codes.definition: Chance may intervene in outer events before the observer's eyes, or during the person's own mental operations such as playing, joking or dreaming.
codes.applies_when: The unexpected input can be identified as coming from an outside event, or from the person's own mental play, joke or dream.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The distinction is between a private occurrence and a large societal event (use 'Personal versus historical contingency').

codes.label: Personal versus historical contingency
codes.definition: Triggering contingencies may happen to the individual privately, such as a mugging. They may also be historical or societal events that affect many people, such as a war.
codes.applies_when: The triggering event is described either as a private personal occurrence or as a large-scale societal or historical event.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The distinction is whether the input came from outer events or from the person's own thinking (use 'External versus internal chance').

codes.label: Idea received from someone else
codes.definition: The venture idea is handed to the person by someone else. This can happen without being sought, as when a friend suggests a business, or through deliberate outside search.
codes.applies_when: The account says the venture idea originally came from another person, whether solicited or unsolicited.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person generated the idea themselves, by accident or by search. Also excluded: a chance meeting that led to a partnership or resource rather than to the idea itself (use 'Chance encounter').

codes.label: Accident from individual side activity
codes.definition: 'Useful weeds' are self-initiated experiments, improvisations or failed projects by individuals inside a firm, pursued for whatever motive, that accidentally yield an innovation.
codes.applies_when: An individual's side experiment, personal tinkering or failed project produced an accidental discovery.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The work was a secret organised group effort against the formal agenda (use 'Skunk work').

codes.label: Skunk work
codes.definition: Individuals or informal groups work voluntarily and secretly on their own initiative, outside or against the formal agenda. Such efforts may bring lucky breaks or disaster.
codes.applies_when: The person describes a secret or unofficial side project, pursued outside official plans, that led to an unexpected breakthrough or venture.
codes.does_not_apply_when: An individual's casual side activity or accident is involved (use 'Accident from individual side activity'). Also excluded: an initiative endorsed by top management.

codes.label: Capabilities built before the opportunity was known
codes.definition: Preadaptation is the accumulation of capabilities before anyone knew of the new application. It is distinguished from adaptation: targeted development after the new opportunity becomes known.
codes.applies_when: The coder can see that relevant skills or resources were built up before the person became aware of the opportunity they later served.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The development was aimed at the opportunity after it was recognised (adaptation), or the account is about general readiness to seize luck (use 'Prepared or self-made luck').

codes.label: Unexpected strategic or managerial value
codes.definition: Unplanned gains in strategy or management that arise beyond the expected benefits, such as new strategic directions, sales channels, revitalised marketing or new acquisition targets.
codes.applies_when: Someone describes an unplanned strategic idea, market approach or management improvement that emerged from a deal or combination.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The unexpected gain concerns technology or product development processes (use 'Unexpected technological value').

codes.label: Unexpected technological value
codes.definition: Unplanned technological gains, such as superior development processes or unexpectedly useful technologies, discovered when engineers from different firms share work.
codes.applies_when: The account reports unexpected learning about technology or development methods through joint engineering work.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The gain is strategic or managerial (use 'Unexpected strategic or managerial value').

codes.label: Kind of thing found
codes.definition: Serendipitous finds take different forms: a person, an institution, or a broadening of one's mental horizon. In discovery more broadly, they may be a new natural resource, a new product or a new productive technique.
codes.applies_when: The account makes clear what was unexpectedly found: a person, an organisation, a new perspective, a resource, a product or a technique.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The interest is in whether the find was the discovery itself or a new use for something existing (use 'Accidental discovery itself' or 'New use for an existing thing').

codes.label: Something odd was noticed
codes.definition: The founder noticed something strange or contrary to expectation, and it led to an idea or a new direction.
codes.applies_when: The founder saw an odd result, behaviour or detail and looked into it instead of ignoring it. For example: 'Customers kept using it for something we never designed it for.'
codes.reason: Suggested core: Odd observation; most-cited trigger (16 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The surprise came from customers or the market as a group (trigger-24), or from a mistake (trigger-04).'

draft_wording.label: Surprising anomalous observation
draft_wording.definition: The person notices a single odd, unexpected result or detail that contradicts what they assumed or what theory predicts, and this provokes curiosity and a new idea or direction. Some authors (following Merton) add that the datum must be strategic, meaning it has wider implications.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account describes noticing something odd, incongruous or contrary to expectation, such as a strange result, irregular data or an unexpected physical effect during work, and then investigating or making sense of it rather than dismissing it.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The odd result came as a by-product while aiming at a different goal and became the new product (use by-product code), or it came from a mistake or mishap (use error code). If the oddity only emerged after many repeated cases, use the repeated-observation code.

codes.label: Repeated surprising observations
codes.definition: An idea emerges only after the same odd occurrence has been met again and again, so that the surprising cases pile up.
codes.applies_when: The person says the idea arose because they kept encountering the same unexpected thing over time.
codes.does_not_apply_when: A single odd detail sparked the idea (use surprising anomalous observation).

codes.label: Weak cue or faint signal
codes.definition: Serendipity is set off by a subtle, peripheral cue, such as a verbal, textual or visual hint or a faint market signal, that most people would overlook but that catches this person's attention.
codes.applies_when: The account stresses that the starting input was subtle, easy to miss or peripheral, and that the person picked it up, linked it to what they knew and followed it up.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The input was striking and plainly contradicted expectations (use surprising anomalous observation), or it was a clear external event such as a crisis or law change.

codes.label: A mistake or accident
codes.definition: An error, slip, malfunction or accident produced something unexpected that turned out to be useful.
codes.applies_when: The founder traces the idea or path to a mistake or mishap. For example: 'We ordered the wrong size by accident and it sold better.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: A planned attempt simply failed and was reused elsewhere. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Mistake or accident. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'A planned attempt simply failed and was reused elsewhere; if no core code fits, use MIS-TRG.'

draft_wording.label: Mistake, accident or mishap
draft_wording.definition: An honest error, accident, slip or sloppy procedure, such as spilling, forgetting, contamination or getting off at the wrong stop, produces something unexpected that turns out to be valuable.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person traces the idea or path to a mistake, accident, malfunction, forgotten item or wrong turn that they then exploited.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: A deliberate attempt worked as carried out but failed at its intended purpose and was found useful elsewhere (use failure turned to another use). The error code is about the slip in the process, not the failed aim.

codes.label: Failure turned to another use
codes.definition: A planned product, experiment or effort fails at its intended purpose or yields something useless, and that failed result is later recognised as valuable for a different use or market.
codes.applies_when: The account tells of a failed experiment, wrong result or useless output (e.g., a mine producing the wrong mineral, a failed insecticide) that became the basis of a new product or business direction.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The surprise came from a slip or accident in carrying out the work (use mistake, accident or mishap), or the unexpected result was a side effect alongside a working main aim (use by-product).

codes.label: By-product of pursuing another goal
codes.definition: While working toward one aim, often under a wrong hypothesis or none at all, the person comes upon an unintended side effect or finding that becomes the main product or a new direction. One author notes this kind of chance arises from the design of the person's own activity rather than from purely outside randomness.
codes.applies_when: The person describes looking for or developing X and encountering an unrelated, valuable Y along the way, such as a side effect in a trial or a strange material in an experiment.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The finding came from the original aim failing (use failure turned to another use) or from an error (use mistake code). If the person was browsing openly with no goal, use undirected browsing.

codes.label: Unplanned action sets off a chain
codes.definition: A short-sighted, unplanned or one-off action or decision, not meant as a step toward an opportunity, starts a chain of reactions that leads the person to stumble into a venture direction or strategy.
codes.applies_when: The account describes an experiment, whim, ad hoc decision or myopic move that unexpectedly snowballed into the venture's direction or became a template for later activity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: A specific unexpected result or side effect was noticed and exploited (use by-product), or the action was a planned step toward an identified opportunity.

codes.label: Constraint, shortage or interruption
codes.definition: A disturbance, scarcity of resources, unlucky constraint or forced pause disrupts what the person was doing and leads to an improvisation, reflection or new idea.
codes.applies_when: The account describes running out of something, having only limited materials, noise or interruption, or an imposed stoppage or wait (e.g., a lab closure) that became the occasion for a new idea.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The disruption was a technical, partner or customer surprise during venture development that forced a change of plan (use unexpected obstacle during development), or a large outside crisis (use external crisis).

codes.label: Unexpected obstacle during development
codes.definition: While building the venture or product, materials, technologies, partners or customers do not behave as planned, and this surprise forces the founders to improvise, learn and change direction.
codes.applies_when: The account describes a snag in carrying out the plan, such as a resource behaving oddly, a technology underperforming, a partner going its own way or a surprise repair need, that redirected development.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The problem came from an industry-wide shift in expectations or an outside crisis (use external crisis), or the surprise was market feedback revealing demand or one's own wrong assumptions (use unexpected market signal).

codes.label: A personal misfortune
codes.definition: An unwanted event in the founder's own life, such as losing a job, illness, bankruptcy or hardship, set off a sequence that led to an opportunity the founder had not planned.
codes.applies_when: The founder tells a personal setback as the starting point, then how acting on it revealed an unexpected need, idea or opening. For example (Harmeling and Sarasvathy 2013, p. 721): after being mugged, a teacher founded a programme teaching business to troubled youth.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The setback hit many people at once. Use "An outside crisis or disaster".
It only pushed the founder into the same work, done for themselves, with no surprise. Leave this code off.
Hardship is mentioned only as background. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Personal misfortune turned into a venture
draft_wording.definition: An unwanted, sometimes traumatic event in the person's own life, such as job loss, bankruptcy, a mugging or hardship, becomes the starting point from which a venture emerges.
draft_wording.applies_when: The founding story begins with a personal setback or misfortune that the person responded to by creating a new venture or opportunity.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The negative event was a broad external crisis affecting many actors (use external crisis), or the setback simply ended activity with nothing made of it.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomaly A33 (a layoff). Stated by Harmeling and Sarasvathy 2013 (pp. 715, 721, 726), which separates a personal contingency from a historical one; Busch 2023 (p. 35, note 12) and Sarasvathy 2001 (p. 247) lean on it.

absorbs.comment: Losing a job set off the path to the venture.

codes.label: An outside crisis or disaster
codes.definition: A sudden, widely shared event outside the venture, such as a recession, market crash, pandemic, natural disaster or war, opened an opportunity, forced a change or threatened the venture.
codes.applies_when: The founder names the event as a reason the venture began, changed course or nearly failed. For example (Williams and Shepherd 2016, p. 2082): after the Haiti earthquake, locals started ventures clearing rubble from streets.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The cause was a new technology, rule or platform. Use "A change in technology, rules or platforms".
The misfortune hit only the founder, such as losing a job. Use "A personal misfortune".
The event is only background or a date. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: External crisis or disaster
draft_wording.definition: A sudden, large outside event such as a pandemic, war, natural disaster, recession, energy crisis or collapse of field-wide expectations creates circumstances that open an opportunity or reshape the venture.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account links a venture's opportunity, new initiative or change in direction to a crisis, accident, disaster or industry-wide jolt that the actors did not create.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The change was a more gradual shift in technology, regulation or tastes (use change in technology, regulation or trends), or the misfortune was personal to the founder (use personal misfortune).

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomalies A22 (first client after a hurricane) and A29 (the 2008 downturn). Stated by Ma 2002 (pp. 526, 529-531), Williams and Shepherd 2016 (pp. 2069, 2080) and Giones et al. 2020 (pp. 3, 5); Garud et al. 2014 (p. 1485) for the threat side. Merton and Barber's Afterword and Mirvahedi and Morrish 2017, attached by the model, do not state it and were dropped.

absorbs.comment: Repair work after Hurricane Sandy, a widely shared disaster, led to the first client.
The 2008 recession hit the venture.

codes.label: A change in technology, rules or platforms
codes.definition: A change outside the founder's control, such as a technology maturing, a rule changing, or a platform or supplier the venture relies on changing its policy, algorithm or product, opened a door or set the venture back.
codes.applies_when: The founder names a specific outside change and ties it to a turn in the story. For example (Garud et al. 2011, p. 753): 3M's light film found its use only when backlit laptop screens arrived; 'the niche found us.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
It was a sudden crisis that hit many people. Use "An outside crisis or disaster".
The change was the founder's own action or one customer's choice. Leave this code off.
It is a vague trend with no named change. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Change in technology, regulation or trends
draft_wording.definition: A change outside the person's control in technology, rules, social trends, tastes or demographics creates or enables an opportunity, sometimes making long-held know-how suddenly viable or relevant. Different people may see different opportunities in the same change.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account traces the venture idea to a new technology, a law or deregulation, a shift in consumer preferences or demographics, a watershed publication, or another outside development that the person then noticed.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The change was a sudden crisis or disaster (use external crisis), or the person created the enabling condition themselves.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomalies A02 and A24 (AI matured), A27 (an iOS update), A31 (a supplier ended a tool) and A34 (a search-engine update). Openings stated by Davidsson 2015 (pp. 675, 684), Davidsson et al. 2020 and Ma 2002 (p. 529); setbacks from platforms stated by Cutolo and Kenney 2021 (pp. 588, 591-592) and Ma 2002 (p. 531). Garud et al. 2011 (p. 753) gives the example.

absorbs.comment: AI tools maturing made the founder's design background suddenly useful.
The maturing of AI made the service possible.
An iOS 14 privacy change cut the venture's ad targeting.
A supplier discontinued an editing tool the product relied on.
A search-engine algorithm update cut the venture's traffic.

codes.label: Right place at the right time
codes.definition: Success comes from happening to be present, nearby or launching at a fortunate moment rather than from planned search. Authors differ: some mean coincidental physical presence or proximity, while others mean that the market happened to be ready, or a short-lived window opened, just when the person acted.
codes.applies_when: The account credits coincidental presence, location or timing, such as being there when something happened, or a market mood or trend that was ripe at launch, or a fleeting opening that had to be seized quickly.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The key element was meeting a particular person (use chance meeting with a person), or a specific outside change is named as the source (use change in technology, regulation or trends).

codes.label: A chance meeting
codes.definition: An unplanned meeting with a person led to a partner, co-founder, customer, investor or opportunity.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes meeting someone by chance: at an event, through a seat on a plane, a shared office. For example: 'I met my co-founder at a wedding.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The meeting was arranged. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Chance meeting; second most-cited trigger (19 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'What mattered was something said in passing rather than the new contact (trigger-17), or the meeting was arranged for a known purpose.'

draft_wording.label: Chance meeting with a person
draft_wording.definition: An unplanned encounter, such as bumping into someone, sitting next to them, meeting at an event, trade fair or hub, or sharing an office, puts the person in contact with someone whose value was not known in advance.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account describes an accidental or casual meeting that led to a new relationship, partner, co-founder, client, expertise or opportunity.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: What mattered was the content of a passing remark rather than the new contact (use offhand remark or suggestion), the contact was an old lapsed tie (use reconnecting with a lapsed contact), or the meeting was deliberately sought for a known purpose.

codes.label: Reconnecting with a lapsed contact
codes.definition: A chance meeting or a mutual friend revives a dormant tie, such as an old classmate or former workmate, and that revived contact passes on crucial information or an opportunity.
codes.applies_when: The person describes running into or being put back in touch with someone they had lost contact with, who then supplied something important.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person met someone new (use chance meeting with a person), or the contact was close and frequently seen.

codes.label: Key person arrives at the right time
codes.definition: A badly needed person, such as a backer, team member, partner or supplier, comes into the venture unexpectedly at a crucial moment and helps turn it into a viable business.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes luckily coming across someone who 'clicked', backed the idea or filled a critical role just when needed, after which things started to move.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The emphasis is on the accidental circumstances of the meeting rather than the person's timely role in the venture (use chance meeting with a person), or the person was recruited through planned processes.

codes.label: A passing remark
codes.definition: A casual comment, question or piece of feedback from someone else revealed a possibility the founder had not seen.
codes.applies_when: The founder says an offhand remark sparked the idea or changed direction. For example: 'My sister said, "you should sell these".'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder read or saw it, rather than hearing it from someone. Use "Came across information by chance".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Offhand remark or suggestion (14 papers); likely frequent in interviews. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The other person made a concrete offer or request (trigger-18), or the value lay in the new relationship (trigger-14).'

draft_wording.label: Offhand remark or suggestion
draft_wording.definition: A casual comment, question, hint, piece of hearsay or feedback from someone else, often an outsider, customer or expert, unexpectedly reveals a possibility, a need or a solution the person had not seen.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account describes a passing remark, overheard conversation, unprompted question, rumour or unexpected reaction that sparked the idea, brought a relevant memory to mind or redirected the venture.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The value lay in forming a new relationship through the meeting (use chance meeting with a person), or the other party made a concrete offer or request (use unsolicited offer or request).

codes.label: An unasked-for offer or request
codes.definition: Someone approached the founder, unsought, with an offer, order, invitation or unusual request, and this started or changed the venture.
codes.applies_when: The founder received an unexpected message, contract, partnership proposal or product request and acted on it. For example: 'A hotel emailed asking if we could make 500.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: Many customers showed a pattern. Use "An unexpected market signal".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Unsolicited offer or request; common for founders. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Unsolicited offer or request
draft_wording.definition: A customer, partner, employer or contact approaches the person without being sought, with an offer of work, money, partnership, an invitation or an unusual request, and this starts or redirects the venture.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account describes receiving an unexpected contract, invitation, message, partnership proposal or product request that the person had not looked for and decided to act on.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Someone merely mentioned a need or idea in passing (use offhand remark or suggestion), or a third party pointed the person to an opportunity or introduced them to someone else (use tip-off or introduction from a third party).

codes.label: Tip-off or introduction from a third party
codes.definition: Someone outside the venture, or a change in the person's network, unexpectedly informs them of an opportunity, recommends them, or links them to a customer or partner.
codes.applies_when: The account describes another actor telling the founder about an opportunity, making a recommendation, or connecting them with a new contact without the founder seeking it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The future partner approached the founder directly with an offer (use unsolicited offer or request), or the founder simply bumped into someone (use chance meeting with a person).

codes.label: Came across information by chance
codes.definition: While doing something else, the founder came across outside information they had not sought, such as an article, a website, a product, a technique, a talk or a sight, and saw what it could mean for them.
codes.applies_when: The founder names the source and says they were not looking for it. For example (von Hippel and von Krogh 2016, pp. 207-208): carrying suitcases through an airport, Sadow saw a worker roll a machine on a wheeled skid, and put wheels on luggage.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
A person said it to the founder in conversation. Use "A passing remark".
The founder was searching for this kind of information. Leave this code off.
The idea came from the founder's own thoughts. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Chance exposure to an outside idea or technology
draft_wording.definition: While doing something else, the person happens upon an invention, technology, text, presentation, media item or sight from an unrelated setting, and sees how it connects to their own capabilities or a need.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes coming across a patent, demo, talk, footnote, TV programme or an incidental scene that sparked an idea or a 'eureka' moment.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The person was deliberately searching for that technology, or was browsing open-endedly as an activity in itself (use undirected browsing).

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomalies A15 (an article), A18 (stumbling on a supplier's website), A32 (a news story) and A10 (a shop that kept catching the founder's eye). Stated by von Hippel and von Krogh 2016 (pp. 207-208) and Shane 2000 (p. 451); Garud et al. 2011 (p. 750) and Krumboltz 1998 (p. 391) give cases. Browsing with no target counts, since the founder was not searching for that information.

absorbs.comment: A vacant shop the founder kept noticing was outside information they had not sought.
A magazine article read by chance sparked the idea.
The founder came across a supplier's website while browsing, not searching.
A chance reading of an article showed blogging as a way to earn.

codes.label: Undirected browsing
codes.definition: Wandering beyond a focused task, such as reading around, walking a trade show 'to see what is new' or exploring byways, exposes the person to chance finds, sometimes revealing a want they did not know they had.
codes.applies_when: The account describes open-ended browsing or exploration that produced an unexpected finding, often 'exactly what I wanted and had not been looking for'.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person was pursuing a specific goal and found something else (use by-product), or met the item by chance without any browsing (use chance exposure to an outside idea or technology).

codes.label: Stumbling on business information
codes.definition: The person comes across valuable business information, such as on competitors or the market, by chance or through unsystematic means rather than through deliberate analysis that others could also do.
codes.applies_when: A founder or manager describes encountering key information unexpectedly while not looking for it, or surprising information that prompted rethinking.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The information was feedback from customers or users about the venture's own offering (use unexpected market signal), or it came from a specific person's remark (use offhand remark or suggestion).

codes.label: Gap left by others' errors or oversight
codes.definition: Earlier mistakes, ignorance or negligence by other market actors leave shortages, mismatches, price discrepancies or unserved needs that the alert person notices and exploits.
codes.applies_when: The person describes noticing a gap, price difference or need that others had failed to serve, or benefiting from a rival's oversight or ignorance.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person discovers an error in their own plans through market feedback (use unexpected market signal).

codes.label: An unexpected market signal
codes.definition: Customers or users responded in a way the founder did not expect: surprising demand, unexpected uses, or feedback showing the plan was wrong.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes a demand spike, a surprising best-seller, or users doing something unforeseen, which pointed to a new path. For example: 'One product we added as an extra outsold everything else.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The surge came from a crisis, such as COVID. Use "An outside crisis or disaster".
The surge came from a new technology, rule or platform. Use "A change in technology, rules or platforms".
One customer asked for it directly. Use "An unasked-for offer or request".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Unexpected customer or user signal; common for founders. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'A single customer made a direct request (trigger-18), or the surprise was a technical problem; if no core code fits, use MIS-TRG.'

draft_wording.label: Unexpected market or user signal
draft_wording.definition: Unanticipated responses from customers or users, such as surprising demand, unexpected usage or market experience showing the plan was wrong, reveal a new use, a profitable product or a better path.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account describes unexpected buying interest, a demand spike, users behaving in unforeseen ways, or market feedback that revealed a different path the person then pursued.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The surprise was a technical or partner snag during development (use unexpected obstacle during development), or a single customer made a direct request (use unsolicited offer or request).

codes.label: Existing solution meets a problem
codes.definition: The person already has a product, skill or remembered idea, and later encounters a problem or everyday annoyance it can address; the answer comes before the question.
codes.applies_when: The person recalls connecting a mundane need or problem with a known but unused technology, skill or idea they already held.
codes.does_not_apply_when: An owned resource turned out to have value in a new context or through an unforeseen synergy without a specific problem prompting it (use resource proves valuable for an unforeseen use), or the person first identified a need and then searched for a solution.

codes.label: Resource proves valuable for an unforeseen use
codes.definition: An asset, skill, product or acquisition obtained for one purpose turns out to be valuable for something else, for example when exposed to new users, settings or conditions, or through a synergy nobody anticipated.
codes.applies_when: The account describes something acquired or made for one reason that later proved useful for a different venture or strategy, or a product used in a new context producing an unexpected effect.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person expected that later use when acquiring it, or a specific problem was matched to a stored solution (use existing solution meets a problem).

codes.label: Idea out of the blue
codes.definition: An idea arrives suddenly and unbidden as a personal insight, sometimes in an incidental setting, through play, a joke, a dream or after a period of forgetting.
codes.applies_when: The person describes a sudden inspiration, whim or realisation, or an idea that came during play or in a dream, as the origin of the venture or product.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person can point to a specific outside observation, remark or event that sparked the idea (use the code for that trigger).

codes.label: General alertness to opportunity
codes.definition: A standing watchfulness or receptiveness to overlooked possibilities, with no specific target in mind. Because of it, the person notices chances that others pass over.
codes.applies_when: The person describes being generally on the lookout, scanning, 'open to the universe' or watching with eyes wide open, and spotting an opportunity as a result.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account describes one specific moment of registering an odd cue; use Noticing and singling out the unexpected. If prior expertise is what made the cue meaningful, use Prepared mind recognising significance.

codes.label: Noticing it
codes.definition: The founder paid attention to something unexpected that others overlooked or would have dismissed.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes the moment they registered a cue and kept it in mind. For example: 'Everyone laughed it off, but I couldn't stop thinking about it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder went on to link it to a need or use. Use "Connecting the dots".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Noticing the unexpected (Busch: trigger noticed). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Noticing and singling out the unexpected
draft_wording.definition: Actively registering an unexpected cue and setting it apart as possibly meaningful, rather than dismissing it as noise or error, often where others saw the same thing and let it pass.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes the moment they paid attention to something odd or peripheral that others overlooked or would have thrown away, and kept it in mind instead of discarding it.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The person goes on to link the cue to a problem or use; use Connecting the dots. If they reinterpret a mistake or nuisance as valuable, use Reframing the unexpected as opportunity.

codes.label: Prepared mind recognising significance
codes.definition: Prior knowledge, theory or long experience lets the person grasp the value of a chance finding (sagacity). Some authors add deliberately building broad background knowledge in advance so as to be ready.
codes.applies_when: The person attributes seeing the value of an unexpected find to their expertise, working hypothesis, years in the field or background knowledge built up beforehand.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person simply perceived something others missed without crediting prior knowledge; use Noticing and singling out the unexpected (one author contrasts theory-led with observer-led noticing). If they put their old skills to work in a new domain, use Redeploying one's own prior knowledge.

codes.label: Generative doubt and questioning assumptions
codes.definition: Acknowledging the limits of one's understanding and holding ideas open to revision, so that preparation is combined with openness to the new. This includes tolerating delay and ambiguity rather than rushing back onto the original track.
codes.applies_when: The person says they did not know, questioned their assumptions, let doubt or ambiguity stand, or let schedules slip in order to understand an unexpected development.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The doubt produces a specific new explanation of an anomaly; use Abductive reasoning about the anomaly.

codes.label: Reframing the unexpected as opportunity
codes.definition: Interpreting a surprise, mistake, nuisance, constraint, setback or dead end as something valuable to build on rather than an error to correct.
codes.applies_when: The person describes coming to see a failure, side effect, accident, difficulty or fruitless contact as an opportunity, or building on an accident instead of fixing it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person deliberately uses a contingency as an input to build the venture without first re-seeing it; use Leveraging contingencies. If they reuse a concrete element from earlier failed work, use Salvaging earlier work and dead ends.

codes.label: Connecting the dots
codes.definition: The founder linked the unexpected input to a need, problem, skill or piece of knowledge, and saw a new idea in the combination (Busch's 'association').
codes.applies_when: The founder describes realising how the new information fit something they knew or needed. For example: 'I put the two together and thought, this could be a product.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder only noticed it, without linking it to anything. Use "Noticing it".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Connecting the dots (Busch: association; 14 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.definition: Forming a mental link between an unexpected input and an existing problem, need, goal or body of knowledge, so that previously unrelated pieces of information make a new idea (bisociation).
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes realising that an unexpected observation or piece of information fit their need, problem, skills or prior knowledge, or that combining it with what they knew revealed an opportunity.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The link is made by carrying a relationship over from another domain; use Analogical transfer. If the person starts from a solution and finds the need it meets, use Matching a solution to an unsought need.

codes.label: Analogical transfer
codes.definition: Seeing a similarity between something in one context or domain and a current problem, and carrying it over as a solution.
codes.applies_when: The person describes something seen in another field, product or nature that suggested a solution by similarity, or an expert pointing to an analogous distant field.
codes.does_not_apply_when: An existing artifact itself is put to a new function; use Repurposing an artifact for a new function.

codes.label: Repurposing an artifact for a new function
