draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: A contact vouches for the entrepreneur or refers customers; use 'Referrals and legitimacy from chance contacts'.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomaly A03 (new contacts on social media). The papers keep contacts and knowledge apart (Klyver et al. 2025, p. 11; Lane et al. 2020, p. 1223), so the draft's merged code was split. Granovetter 1973 (p. 1372) and Soto's chapter in Copeland et al. 2023 (p. 213) state contacts as what chance brings. Resources such as a supplier or a loan have no paper that states them and stay anomalies.

absorbs.comment: New connections found the founder through consistent branding on social media.

codes.label: Referrals and legitimacy from chance contacts
codes.definition: Former strangers vouch for the entrepreneur and refer clients or contacts, sometimes in chains of new customers.
codes.applies_when: A once-unknown contact refers customers, makes introductions or lends credibility.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The contact supplies resources directly; use 'Resources and help from chance encounters'.

codes.label: New knowledge
codes.definition: What came of the unexpected event was knowledge, advice or ideas the founder used later, rather than a product, a market or growth.
codes.applies_when: The founder says the event taught them something they then used. For example (Lane et al. 2020, p. 1239): scientists who met by chance learned about outside work and used it in their own research.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The idea itself became the product. Use "A new product or service".
The event changed the founder's whole way of seeing things, not just their know-how. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Learning and new knowledge
draft_wording.definition: Chance discoveries and encounters produce new know-how, information or improved practice that the person brings into later work.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person reports gaining knowledge, advice, methods or practice improvements from an unexpected event or a former stranger.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The event changed the person's basic way of seeing or theorising; use 'Changed thinking or new framework'.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomaly A14 (customer calls full of ideas). Split from the draft's merged code. Stated by Lane et al. 2020 (p. 1239) and Klyver et al. 2025 (p. 11); Fultz and Hmieleski 2025 (p. 1572) call new knowledge serendipity's main output.

absorbs.comment: Customer calls gave the founders a stock of ideas they used later.

codes.label: Changed thinking or new framework
codes.definition: An unexpected result reshapes how the person thinks: it breaks assumptions, opens new questions, yields a new idea or theory, or reorients later decisions.
codes.applies_when: The person says an unexpected event changed how they think or decide, challenged established assumptions, or generated a new idea, hypothesis or line of inquiry.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The gain is specific know-how or information; use 'Learning and new knowledge'.

codes.label: Confidence and entrepreneurial identity
codes.definition: Unexpected events and the venture's unfolding build self-confidence, belief in one's own agency and an entrepreneurial identity, sometimes through inspiring strangers. These traits arise as an effect of entrepreneurship rather than only as its cause.
codes.applies_when: The person describes becoming more confident, entrepreneurial or agentic, or changing their self-concept, after an unexpected event or encounter.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confidence comes from reading chance performance as proof the strategy works; use 'Strategy reinforced or changed by misread luck'.

codes.label: Strategy reinforced or changed by misread luck
codes.definition: Chance outcomes are misread as evidence about strategy. Leaders become more confident in their strategy, while laggards change theirs.
codes.applies_when: The venture keeps or abandons a strategy because of results that may have come from chance.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The change concerns personal identity or self-belief; use 'Confidence and entrepreneurial identity'.

codes.label: Pleasure and morale boost
codes.definition: Serendipitous finds bring delight, amazement or awe and raise morale. This can make even small finds feel significant.
codes.applies_when: The person expresses delight, wonder or energised spirits about a timely, unexpected good outcome.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person feels uneasy about the luck; use 'Discomfort with undeserved success'.

codes.label: Discomfort with undeserved success
codes.definition: Unexpected good fortune can bring moral unease and self-doubt, and the risk that others will dismiss the success as mere luck.
codes.applies_when: The person expresses unease, self-doubt or fear of others' judgment after a lucky success.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The reaction is positive delight; use 'Pleasure and morale boost'.

codes.label: Value requires conversion work
codes.definition: Serendipity creates only potential value. It has to be converted through effort, capability and extensive development before it pays off.
codes.applies_when: The account stresses the work, capability or long development needed to turn a lucky break into value.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Success depended on users or markets accepting the innovation; use 'Market acceptance required'.

codes.label: Market acceptance required
codes.definition: A serendipitous or novel offering succeeds only if others adopt it. This often requires educating customers or reworking the concept.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes customers not understanding the offering, missionary work, or success depending on uptake by users.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The effort was internal development of the discovery; use 'Value requires conversion work'.

codes.label: Nothing came of it
codes.definition: The unexpected opportunity was missed, dismissed, dropped or forgotten.
codes.applies_when: The founder recounts a chance signal or contact they ignored or did not follow up, sometimes with regret. For example: 'Someone offered to invest early on and I said no.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: It caused harm or loss. Use "Harm or loss".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Nothing came of it: missed or dropped; needed so outcome is not only success. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The find was pursued and led somewhere; use the outcome codes for what it led to.'

draft_wording.label: Missed or forgotten serendipity
draft_wording.definition: An unexpected opportunity is not noticed, dismissed, or noticed but never pursued. Or it is never embedded in routines and is forgotten, sometimes followed by regret.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person recounts an unexpected signal, insight or connection that was overlooked, ignored, not acted on or forgotten, or regret over it.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The discovery was shelved for lack of support, or later exploited by others; use 'Stalled or exploited by others'.

codes.label: Stalled or exploited by others
codes.definition: A recognised serendipitous finding stalls for years for lack of resources or support. Or it is so unexpected that a different party, not the discoverer, capitalises on it.
codes.applies_when: A chance discovery is shelved or delayed, or is later revived or exploited by another person or firm.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The discovery was simply never noticed or pursued by anyone; use 'Missed or forgotten serendipity'.

codes.label: Cascade of further opportunities
codes.definition: One serendipitous outcome opens new possibilities that lead to further unexpected opportunities and widening applications over time.
codes.applies_when: The speaker describes one unexpected find or first move leading to later, often larger, unforeseen opportunities or applications.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account is about the idea spreading through others' networks; use 'Unplanned spread and uptake'.

codes.label: Unplanned spread and uptake
codes.definition: A small initiative unexpectedly spreads through others' networks, bringing inquiries, adoption, awards or press that were never planned.
codes.applies_when: The person describes their idea or venture being picked up widely in ways they did not anticipate.
codes.does_not_apply_when: New opportunities follow from one's own discoveries; use 'Cascade of further opportunities'.

codes.label: Distraction and loss of focus
codes.definition: Chasing serendipity can cause drift, opportunity overload, scattered ad hoc ideas, derailment from the task, or lost efficiency on the original plan.
codes.applies_when: The person describes unexpected opportunities distracting them, clouding direction, scattering effort, causing delays or trading off against efficient delivery.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The unexpected event caused direct harm, losses or errors; use 'Harmful or costly unexpected outcomes'.

codes.label: Harm or loss
codes.definition: An unplanned event outside the founder's control cost the venture something concrete: sales, income, a channel, money or its chances of survival.
codes.applies_when: The founder says a surprise hurt the venture in concrete terms, even if they later recovered. For example (Brownell et al. 2024, p. 1711): bad luck can prevent a new venture's success.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
A chance was simply missed. Use "Nothing came of it".
The only cost was time or focus. Leave this code off.
The loss came from the founder's own planned choice, with no unexpected event. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Harmful or costly unexpected outcomes
draft_wording.definition: Most accidents are not valuable. Openness to chance or bold action on a perceived opportunity can produce costly errors, losses, misinformation or harmful consequences (zemblanity).
draft_wording.applies_when: The person notes chance outcomes that were useless, harmful or costly, or a misread opportunity that led to losses.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The cost is lost focus or direction; use 'Distraction and loss of focus'.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomalies A28 (a sales channel lost), A30 (survival threatened) and A35 (income halved). Brownell et al. 2024 define luck as having beneficial or harmful consequences (p. 1685) and say bad luck can prevent new venture success (p. 1711); Giustiniano et al. 2016 (p. 8) name the harmful side zemblanity. The papers the model attached only lean on it and were dropped.

absorbs.comment: A post that brought customers was deleted by a new moderator, and the channel was lost.
The recession threatened the venture's survival.
The search-engine update halved the founder's income.

codes.label: Valuable by-product of other work
codes.definition: Work aimed at something else, including failed projects and apparent mistakes, incidentally yields a valuable side result, feature, application or spillover.
codes.applies_when: The person reports a benefit that arose incidentally from an initiative with another purpose, or from something once judged a failure.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The benefit was the initiative's explicit goal, or the gain came from buying an undervalued resource; use 'Windfall gain from undervalued resources'.

codes.label: Venture mirrors founder's background
codes.definition: Opportunities that arrive by chance or through networks tend to produce ventures close to the founder's prior industry and knowledge, which imprint the venture's market and model.
codes.applies_when: The venture is an offshoot of the founder's prior work, or its form or market reflects their background.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The chance event redirected the founder into a different career or line of work; use 'Redirection of venture or career'.

codes.label: Chance deals crowd out planning
codes.definition: Relying on deals that arrive unplanned reduces later effort to build planned capabilities such as a sales function.
codes.applies_when: The founder relied on incoming deals rather than building sales or planning functions.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Chance opportunities caused distraction rather than neglect of capability building; use 'Distraction and loss of focus'.

codes.label: Redirection of venture or career
codes.definition: An unplanned development redirects the venture or the person's professional life. It may take them into new areas, lead to an additional venture, or turn out to be a misstep later abandoned.
codes.applies_when: The person describes a chance event changing the venture's direction or their career, starting an extra venture, or a discounted idea succeeding and prompting a change of course.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The unexpected input kept the project on its original course; use 'Project kept on its original path'.

codes.label: Stalled work unblocked
codes.definition: A chance encounter or insight supplies the missing piece, so that long-stalled work moves forward quickly.
codes.applies_when: The person reports that after a chance meeting or insight, a difficult problem was solved and the rest followed quickly.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The chance input only explained a crisis so the team could continue as before; use 'Project kept on its original path'.

codes.label: Project kept on its original path
codes.definition: An unexpected explanation resolves a crisis, so the project survives without changing direction.
codes.applies_when: An unexpected input lets the team return to its original assumptions and continue rather than end the project.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The input leads to new assumptions and a new direction; use 'Redirection of venture or career'.

codes.label: Greater openness to future chance
codes.definition: Implemented serendipitous discoveries make people more alert and receptive to the unexpected. Failed ones teach self-censorship.
codes.applies_when: Past success or failure with unexpected ideas is described as shaping later openness to them.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The organisation builds formal routines to exploit the unexpected; use 'Serendipity becomes a dynamic capability'.

codes.label: Environment transformed
codes.definition: Ventures built from contingencies end up changing the institutions and conditions in which the original contingencies arose.
codes.applies_when: The venture is described as changing the institutions or conditions around it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The venture creates a new market; use 'New market, industry or field created'.

codes.label: Delayed payoff
codes.definition: Benefits from chance encounters may emerge only slowly, after years.
codes.applies_when: The person notes that the benefits of a chance meeting appeared long after it happened.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The finding was shelved for lack of support; use 'Stalled or exploited by others'.

codes.label: Told as if planned
codes.definition: Looking back, the founder tells an unplanned, chance-filled path as an orderly plan, smoothing over or leaving out the unexpected turns.
codes.applies_when: The story is told as linear or intended, while the details show unplanned turns. For example: 'We always knew this was the market', though earlier they describe stumbling into it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder credits their own skill but tells the events in order. Use "Credited to effort, not luck".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Chance told as a planned story (18 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The founder credits success to their own skill rather than recasting the sequence; if no core code fits, use MIS-ACC.'

draft_wording.label: Chance airbrushed into a planned story
draft_wording.definition: Looking back, the person tells an unplanned, chance-laden process as an orderly, purposeful or logical sequence that was intended from the start. Unexpected events are left out, minimised or reshaped, sometimes deliberately and sometimes through unaware recall bias.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account presents the founding or a discovery as planned, linear or inevitable while its details show unplanned turns, or the person admits that chance was smoothed over or left out of how the story is usually told.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Lucky success credited to skill' when the point is crediting the outcome to personal capability rather than recasting the sequence of events as planned. Use 'Failed chance leads go untold' when the issue is omitted dead ends.

codes.label: Failed chance leads go untold
codes.definition: Serendipity stories are rebuilt backwards from successes. Accidents and chance leads that went nowhere, and failed attempts along the way, drop out of the telling.
codes.applies_when: The account presents only the chance event that worked, or the person acknowledges that other accidents, failed attempts or unpursued leads are not usually mentioned.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance airbrushed into a planned story' when chance itself is removed. Here chance stays in the story, but only the successful instances are told.

codes.label: Chance inflated or dramatised
codes.definition: In retrospect, people make a story sound more serendipitous than it was, to convey excitement or significance or to make a good story. Such stories can become legends or myths. Authors note that retrospective accounts can either inflate or erase chance; this code covers inflation.
codes.applies_when: The person tells a dramatised, legendary or embellished chance story, especially for an audience, or the story seems built after the fact around a chance turning point.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance story hides prior groundwork' when the main point is that preparation or effort behind the event is left out, rather than that the chance element is exaggerated.

codes.label: Chance story hides prior groundwork
codes.definition: The account credits a single lucky moment or an effortless tip, while long prior work, search, background interests or problem framing that made the discovery likely stay hidden. The search and the result appear immediately linked.
codes.applies_when: The person tells of a lucky, effortless or obvious-in-hindsight discovery, while the account reveals earlier groundwork, an existing problem or need, a background interest, or effort and expertise behind it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance inflated or dramatised' when the story exaggerates or invents chance without hiding identifiable prior work.

codes.label: Lucky success credited to skill
codes.definition: After a success, the person explains it mainly by their own capability, strategy, foresight, alertness or distinctive history. The role of chance and early lucky breaks is played down or left out.
codes.applies_when: The narrator credits success wholly or mainly to skill, vision, competence or something special in the venture's history, while the events described point to luck. This includes holding up a run of success as proof of superiority.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck framed as earned or deserved' when luck is acknowledged but presented as merited. Use 'Claimed hunch or intuition' when success is credited specifically to gut feeling.

codes.label: Claimed hunch or intuition
codes.definition: Afterwards the person says they had a hunch, gut feeling or conviction that led them to the right choice. Authors note such claims cannot be verified and may disguise a chance hit.
codes.applies_when: The person says they 'knew all along', had a hunch before the unexpected event, or succeeded through intuition or single-minded conviction rather than analysis.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Mystical or fated explanation' when the instinct is presented as uncanny or inexplicable, like a sixth sense, rather than as personal intuition.

codes.label: Skill for successes, bad luck for failures
codes.definition: The person credits successes to their own skill, instinct or providence and blames failures on bad luck, other people or outside factors.
codes.applies_when: Within the same account, good outcomes are credited to the self or to providence and bad outcomes to chance or to others.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Lucky success credited to skill' when only successes are discussed and there is no shifting of blame for failures.

codes.label: Credited to luck
codes.definition: The founder explicitly explains an event or success as luck, chance or being in the right place at the right time.
codes.applies_when: The founder uses luck language. For example: 'Honestly, we just got lucky.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder splits credit between luck and their own effort. Use "Part luck, part effort".
The founder says the opportunity came to them, not that they were lucky. Use "The opportunity found them".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Explained as luck. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Outcome explained as luck
draft_wording.definition: The person explicitly attributes an outcome to luck, chance, fortune, a happy accident or being in the right place at the right time. Often luck is invoked as a brief explanation for something otherwise unexplained.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account uses luck, chance, fate, fortune, happy accident or right-place-right-time language to explain an event or success, including as a side comment or to explain why effort and results did not match.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Mix of luck and own effort' when the person apportions success between luck and skill. Use 'Modest credit to luck' when the luck attribution is self-effacing.

codes.label: Part luck, part effort
codes.definition: The founder divides credit between luck and their own skill or hard work.
codes.applies_when: The founder says success was partly luck and partly effort, or that they made their own luck. For example: 'Luck opened the door, but we worked hard to walk through it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder credits luck alone. Use "Credited to luck".
The founder credits effort and plays luck down. Use "Credited to effort, not luck".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Mix of luck and own effort. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Mix of luck and own effort
draft_wording.definition: The person divides credit between luck and their own skill, foresight or hard work, sometimes giving proportions. They may describe the venture's origins as partly designed and partly coincidental, or say success needs both 'pluck and luck'.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person says success was part luck and part effort, gives a share or percentage of luck, describes origins as a mix of planned steps and coincidences, or says they make their own luck while admitting chance mattered.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck framed as earned or deserved' when luck is acknowledged mainly in order to defend it as merited.

codes.label: Luck framed as earned or deserved
codes.definition: The person acknowledges good luck but defends it as earned, deserved or the reward of preparation and effort. They may balance it against past misfortune, or ask whether they deserved it.
codes.applies_when: The narrator insists a lucky outcome was earned, stresses the striving that the chance event multiplied, says chance comes only to the deserving, points to earlier bad luck as making good luck due, or justifies a lucky find to peers or stakeholders.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Lucky success credited to skill' when luck is not acknowledged at all.

codes.label: Luck as happening to me versus achieved by me
codes.definition: The person frames a chance discovery either as a windfall that passively happened to them or as something they actively accomplished through alertness, effort or acting on contingency. They may also waver between the two.
codes.applies_when: The account shows whether a lucky find is told as an unearned gift or windfall, or as the product of the person's own alertness, imagination and action. This includes separating credit for planned results from credit for surprises.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck framed as earned or deserved' when the person is defending the legitimacy of the luck rather than describing their own role in bringing the find about.

codes.label: Modest credit to luck
codes.definition: The person attributes their own success to luck in a self-deprecating way. This may be genuine belief or a narrative device to appear humble to an audience.
codes.applies_when: The person says they were 'just lucky' about their own achievement, especially in a way that downplays their own role or talent, or seems aimed at investors or other listeners.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Outcome explained as luck' when luck is credited plainly, without a self-effacing tone.

codes.label: Chance seen as discrediting
codes.definition: Chance-based success or a winding, unplanned path is treated as a sign of undeserved reward, passivity, lack of strategy or incompetence. This can lead the person to worry that it lessens their credit, or to apologise for it.
codes.applies_when: The person or others treat accidental success as less worthy ('anybody could have done that'), worry that calling something luck reduces their credit, apologise for or justify a nonlinear path, or report being seen as lacking strategy for chasing opportunities.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck framed as earned or deserved' when the person actively defends the luck as merited, rather than describing the stigma itself.

codes.label: Natural knack for lucky finds
codes.definition: The person presents themselves as someone with an innate gift, or a career marked by repeated valuable unexpected finds, and takes pride in the aura of good fortune.
codes.applies_when: The person says they have a knack, gift or natural talent for lucky finds, or describes their career or method as a series of valuable unsought discoveries in a way that presents them as specially fortunate.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Mystical or fated explanation' when the finds are credited to outside forces or an inexplicable sixth sense rather than to a personal trait.

codes.label: Mystical or fated explanation
codes.definition: A fortunate coincidence is explained by fate, providence, destiny, a guiding force or an inexplicable sixth sense. This avoids deciding whether skill or plain chance was responsible.
codes.applies_when: The person invokes fate, destiny, mysterious forces, an uncanny instinct, a 'radar' or premonition to explain an opportunity or repeated lucky finds.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Outcome explained as luck' when plain chance is invoked without any suggestion of mysterious or guiding forces.

codes.label: Eureka moment and excited recall
codes.definition: The discovery is told as a sudden flash, an 'aha' or a 'click', or as sudden clarity after waiting. It is recalled vividly, with surprise and elation.
codes.applies_when: The person recounts a sudden moment of realisation, an instant fit with someone after which things started to roll, or a find told with marked excitement, vivid detail or a shift to positive feeling.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Serendipity as gradual build-up' when the discovery is told as unfolding over time through many moments.

codes.label: Serendipity as gradual build-up
codes.definition: Serendipity is told not as a single flash but as a series of accidents, a slow crescendo, or a long and partly controlled exploration over an extended period.
codes.applies_when: The person describes the discovery as building up gradually through many chance moments or a protracted, effortful exploration.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Eureka moment and excited recall' when a single sudden insight is described.

codes.label: Only clear in hindsight
codes.definition: The founder says the event seemed minor at the time and only later proved to be a turning point.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes something that seemed small or unimportant then but crucial now. For example: 'I almost didn't go to that meetup.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: A setback first seen as bad luck was later seen differently. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Significance seen only in hindsight. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'What was reinterpreted was a setback first seen as bad luck; if no core code fits, use MIS-ACC.'

draft_wording.label: Significance seen only in hindsight
draft_wording.definition: The person realises only looking back that an encounter, piece of information or decision was a turning point or the genesis of the venture. At the time it seemed minor, unhelpful or was made for other reasons.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person says something seemed minor, was dismissed, or was chosen for unrelated reasons, but in retrospect proved crucial or 'turned out' lucky. This includes 'you never know where it leads' framing.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Setback reframed as fortunate' when what is reinterpreted was originally seen as bad luck rather than as unimportant.

codes.label: Setback reframed as fortunate
codes.definition: An event first seen as bad luck, a mistake or a failure is later retold as good luck, a learning opportunity, or a solution looking for a problem. Authors differ: some call this repackaging misfortune, others defend it as genuine reappraisal.
codes.applies_when: The person narrates a setback, mistake or failed result that in hindsight they describe as lucky, as something they learned from or that made them stronger, or as useful but with an unknown use.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Significance seen only in hindsight' when the earlier event was seen as trivial, not as bad.

codes.label: Making meaning of surprises
codes.definition: The person works out the meaning of events while acting or afterwards, retells the past in a new light to fit changed circumstances, and constructs surprises either as meaningful and happening for a reason or as random noise.
codes.applies_when: The account shows goals or meaning becoming clear only during or after action, the past being renarrated to justify a new direction, or a surprise being framed as either a meaningful lesson or a random deviation.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Setback reframed as fortunate' when what is specifically reinterpreted is bad luck turned into good luck.

codes.label: Would not have happened otherwise
codes.definition: The person reflects counterfactually that the venture or connection would not have happened without the chance event, for example without being co-located, or because they had never thought of the idea.
codes.applies_when: The account asks 'would it have happened if…', credits the connection to proximity or membership, or says they would otherwise be doing something else.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Venture just happened to me' when the emphasis is on never having intended to found a business rather than on the event being necessary.

codes.label: The opportunity found them
codes.definition: The founder tells the start as something that came to them, such as people asking to buy or an offer, while they were not looking for a business, and does not call it luck.
codes.applies_when: The founder says the venture happened to them or found them. For example (Shah and Tripsas 2007, p. 131): 'I was approached by mothers wanting to know where they could buy one… so I started a company.'
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder explains the start as luck or chance. Use "Credited to luck".
The founder searched for an opportunity. Leave this code off.

draft_wording.label: Venture just happened to me
draft_wording.definition: Founders narrate the founding as unintended, as something that happened to them or as the opportunity finding them. They express surprise at having become an entrepreneur at all.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person says they never intended to start a business, never saw themselves as an entrepreneur, or that 'it found us' or 'it just happened'.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck as happening to me versus achieved by me' when the framing concerns a particular discovery rather than the founding and the person's identity as a founder.

codes.change_note: Round 1 anomaly A11 (the founder tells the start as the opportunity finding them). Stated by Shah and Tripsas 2007 (pp. 126, 131) and Mirvahedi and Morrish 2017 (p. 190). The model attached Baker and Nelson 2003, Garud et al. 2011 and Reijonen 2023; they were not read for this code and were replaced.

absorbs.comment: The founder tells the start as the opportunity finding them.

codes.label: The right moment
codes.definition: Success is narrated in terms of timing: the right opportunity appearing when the time was right, or choosing the moment when circumstances aligned and 'the time was ripe'.
codes.applies_when: The person explains a decision, launch or opportunity by waiting for the right moment, ripeness or the alignment of circumstances.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Outcome explained as luck' when 'right place, right time' is used as a luck idiom rather than as an account of timing and waiting.

codes.label: Cannot trace where it came from
codes.definition: Because of delays between trigger and insight, people cannot recall or properly attribute the original source of an idea. They may also acknowledge debts to chance conversations or readings that they cannot reconstruct.
codes.applies_when: The person cannot pinpoint or date where an idea or connection came from, gives vague origins, or says chance encounters shaped things in ways they cannot fully reconstruct.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance story hides prior groundwork' when a specific origin is given but earlier work is omitted.

codes.label: Under my very nose
codes.definition: The person describes the discovery as surprise at their own earlier ignorance: what they found had been available all along.
codes.applies_when: The person says 'it was right in front of me' or expresses surprise at not having seen it before.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Missed earlier chances' when the person regrets a specific delayed encounter rather than an overlooked opportunity.

codes.label: Missed earlier chances
codes.definition: Looking back, the person regrets that a key encounter did not happen sooner, although the chance had been there many times.
codes.applies_when: The narrator says they passed the key person or chance many times before acting and wishes it had happened earlier.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Under my very nose' when the focus is on surprise at an overlooked opportunity rather than regret about lost time.

codes.label: Official versus personal versions
codes.definition: The same venture story exists in different versions. Formal, official or outside analysts' accounts streamline events and expurgate accidents, while insiders' informal retellings restore the miscalculations, surprises and luck.
codes.applies_when: The person contrasts their own insider account with an official, formal or analyst version, or recounts chance episodes absent from the official story, or notes that formal accounts omit the accidents.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance airbrushed into a planned story' when there is a single account that smooths chance out, with no contrast between versions.

codes.label: Chance stories as shared lore
codes.definition: People enjoy telling and retelling serendipity tales, and one tale prompts another. Within organisations, stories of stumbling onto discoveries become memory that inspires and legitimises new pursuits.
codes.applies_when: The account retells accidental-discovery stories as models for how innovation happens, as company lore, or as tales worth telling, or one chance story prompts another.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Serendipity used to justify exploration' when the stories are aimed at investors or sponsors to justify spending.

codes.label: Serendipity used to justify exploration
codes.definition: Firms and researchers invoke chance-discovery stories to investors, sponsors or the public as proof that unplanned exploration pays off. They present leaving room for accidents as deliberate strategy.
codes.applies_when: The person tells investors or stakeholders that accidental discoveries are a route to returns, or uses chance stories to justify exploratory spending.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Chance stories as shared lore' when stories circulate internally as inspiration without being used to persuade funders.

codes.label: Credit given to a lone hero
codes.definition: A collective, partly lucky process is retold as the merit or insight of one individual founder or discoverer.
codes.applies_when: Credit for a breakthrough or success goes to one person, while the narrative reveals multiple contributors, interactions or luck.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Lucky success credited to skill' when the issue is crediting capability over chance without collapsing a group's contribution into one person.

codes.label: Same event, different framings
codes.definition: Whether an event is told as serendipity depends on the narrator's perspective, emphasis and values. It can be serendipitous for one party but goal-directed for another, or read as accident by some and as plan by others.
codes.applies_when: Different people describe the same event as accident versus plan, one party deliberately sought what the other experienced as unexpected, or a narrator's interpretation of chance plainly reflects their wider values.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Official versus personal versions' when the contrast is between a formal or outside account and an insider's account of the same venture.

codes.label: Opportunity told as discovered or created
codes.definition: After the fact, an opportunity can be told as found because it was always there, or as made through the person's own framing and effort, or as both.
codes.applies_when: The founder narrates the opportunity as having been there all along, flowing logically from an existing industry, or as both found and made through their own framing.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use 'Luck as happening to me versus achieved by me' when the framing concerns the person's role in a lucky event rather than the nature of the opportunity itself.

codes.label: Pure luck, no action
codes.definition: A good thing happened to the founder by chance, and they describe no noticing, judging or acting of their own. This is luck, not serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The founder presents an event as a windfall that simply happened. For example: 'A big blog wrote about us out of nowhere and sales took off.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder also noticed the event and acted on it. Use "Agency: acted on it".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Main look-alike: luck without agency (22 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The founder also describes noticing and acting on the event; then it may be serendipity, and this rival does not apply.'

draft_wording.label: Pure luck without agency
draft_wording.definition: A fortunate event is explained as chance, fortune, accident, fate or providence alone, with no noticing, recognising or acting by the person. Most authors present this as distinct from serendipity, which needs the person's sagacity and response.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person narrates a favourable event or find as something that just happened to them (a happy accident, a windfall, sheer luck) and describes no search, preparedness, recognition or follow-up of their own.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Venture performance as random luck': use that code when the claim concerns the venture's overall survival, growth or results being driven by random variation, not a single fortunate event. Do not use when the person also describes noticing and acting on the chance event.

codes.label: Venture performance as random luck
codes.definition: Differences in venture survival, growth or profitability are explained as the luck of the draw, random shocks, timing or external conditions rather than founders' skills or actions. Authors differ: some argue luck should be the default explanation, while others criticise this view or hold that chance events are spread evenly and cannot by themselves explain performance.
codes.applies_when: The account attributes the venture's overall results, survival, failure or growth mainly to chance, random shocks, timing or uncontrollable conditions, or to the market being so ambiguous that results were a game of luck.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Pure luck without agency', which concerns a single fortunate event. Also confused with 'Compounding early advantage or privilege': use that code when an initial lucky break or privilege is said to have snowballed over time.

codes.label: Compounding early advantage or privilege
codes.definition: Success is traced to advantaged starting conditions, such as inherited wealth, social connections, early luck or early success, that were amplified over time through path dependence or rich-get-richer dynamics, rather than to serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The account shows that a privileged start, an early lucky break or initial success opened doors (for example investor contacts or extra resources) that then drove later success or survival, or that lock-in followed an initial chance event without anyone actively seizing it.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Superior resources or complementary assets', which credits resources or capabilities treated as the firm's genuine strengths rather than as advantages that luck or privilege handed out and then compounded.

codes.label: Foresight or insight rather than chance
codes.definition: An apparently lucky outcome is explained by the actor's better information, foresight, anticipation, guiding idea, insight or sagacity, so that chance was at most an accompanying circumstance.
codes.applies_when: The person credits the outcome to knowing or anticipating something others did not, to a prior theory or vision, to deliberate study of trends, to analogy, to reflection on their own unique skills, or to acute insight. Also use when the outcome is framed as foreseen or predicted, or when what looked like luck is said to reflect expertise or structural position.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search', which centres on a structured process of looking for an opportunity or solution rather than on superior anticipation or insight. Also confused with 'Opportunity discovered by alertness', which concerns a general readiness to notice rather than specific foresight.

codes.label: Superior resources or complementary assets
codes.definition: Success or a profitable acquisition is explained by the firm's better starting resources, human capital, market position, commercialisation assets, or an unusually good fit between a new resource and what the firm already had. One author notes the objection that complementarity may itself reduce to luck.
codes.applies_when: The account credits outcomes to superior resources, experienced management, the founders' prior industry knowledge and skills, distribution or manufacturing assets, an attractive industry position, or a fit with existing assets that few others could match.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Foresight or insight rather than chance', which credits knowing or anticipating something rather than possessing assets. Also confused with 'Compounding early advantage or privilege', which treats the advantage as luck or privilege amplified over time.

codes.label: Systematic search
codes.definition: The opportunity came from a planned, methodical search with no real surprise: researching markets, testing ideas, working from a known problem.
codes.applies_when: The founder decided what to look for and found it as expected. For example: 'I analysed 40 niches and picked the one with the best margins.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The search was under way, but the answer came unexpectedly. Use "Searching for something specific".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Main look-alike: systematic search (22 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Not when was: 'The search was under way but the answer came unexpectedly; that is serendipity, not this rival (see definition-04).'

draft_wording.label: Deliberate systematic search
draft_wording.definition: The opportunity, solution or discovery is explained as the planned result of goal-directed search: scanning markets, defined problem-solving, structured idea generation, or designed tests, with little or no unexpected input.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes deciding what they were looking for and then methodically searching, researching, scanning, interviewing, testing hypotheses or working from an identified problem to a solution that turned out as expected. This includes deciding to start a business first and then searching for what to start.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Chance find for an existing goal', where search was under way but the answer came unexpectedly or from an unexpected place. Also confused with 'Planned strategy execution', which concerns carrying out a plan or strategy rather than searching for an opportunity.

codes.label: A plan carried out
codes.definition: The venture's founding or growth is explained as a plan or strategy carried out as intended.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes following a plan made in advance, step by step, without unexpected turns. For example: 'We had a five-year plan and stuck to it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The point is how the idea was searched for. Use "Systematic search".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Main look-alike: a plan carried out (16 papers). Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Planned strategy execution
draft_wording.definition: Outcomes are explained as the realisation of prior intentions, such as a formulated strategy, a vision or a staged plan carried out as intended, or coordinated directed effort, including rational evaluation of alternatives. Some authors include tacit shared intentions behind developments that look accidental.
draft_wording.applies_when: The account presents the venture's founding or development as following a plan made in advance, a rational choice among alternatives, a grand vision, a structured staged programme, or explicit or shared intentions realised without unexpected deviation. This includes success explained after the fact as the result of deliberate strategy.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search', which concerns how the opportunity itself was looked for. Also confused with 'Environmentally imposed direction', where outside forces rather than the actors' intentions set the course.

codes.label: Chance find for an existing goal
codes.definition: Something found by chance, or in an unexpected place, served a goal the person already held, so on a narrow view it is pseudo-serendipity or not serendipity at all. Authors differ: some reserve serendipity for cases where the objective changed, while Busch and Grimes reject this narrow view.
codes.applies_when: The person was already on the lookout for a solution of that kind, and the unexpected find advanced that same goal without changing their objective.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search', where the answer came as expected from the search itself. Do not use when the find changed what the person was trying to do.

codes.label: Deliberate incremental extension or iteration
codes.definition: A new use or venture idea is explained as the planned extension of an existing technology to adjacent targets, improvement within the same domain, or planned cycles of prototyping and reformulating the problem.
codes.applies_when: The account describes systematically trying a product on closely related problems or markets, making a technology more efficient or robust within its original field, or reaching the idea through planned iterative prototype testing with users.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search', which looks for an opportunity from scratch rather than stepwise extension or iteration of something existing. Do not use when the technology was moved to an unexpected new field through a chance encounter.

codes.label: Working with what's at hand
codes.definition: The venture is explained as the founder combining resources, skills or contacts they already had, with no unexpected trigger (effectuation, bricolage).
codes.applies_when: The founder describes building from their own means, making do and recombining, and reports no surprise. For example: 'I had a van and some carpentry skills, so I started there.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: An unexpected event that the founder noticed is also there, which points to serendipity. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Effectuation and bricolage as rivals; common in founder stories. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Label was: 'Working with what was at hand'; Not when was: 'An unexpected event and its recognition are also present; then this supports serendipity rather than replacing it.'

draft_wording.label: Means-driven processes
draft_wording.definition: Ventures are explained by starting from resources, knowledge or solutions already at hand and deliberately combining them or looking for problems to apply them to. This covers effectuation, bricolage, knowledge recombination, improvisation and garbage-can linking, without an unexpected triggering event.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes working with available means, making do with what was at hand, deliberately recombining existing knowledge with new inputs, or matching already articulated problems with available solutions, and reports no surprise or unexpected trigger.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search', which starts from a defined problem or goal rather than from existing means. If an unexpected event and its recognition are present, these processes support serendipity rather than replace it.

codes.label: Routines rather than chance
codes.definition: Apparently fortunate connections or foundings are explained by established routines, such as a serial founder's familiar founding approach or organisational practices that systematically produce new combinations.
codes.applies_when: The account attributes the connection or founding to repeated, systematic practices, for example brainstorms, knowledge catalogues, deliberate involvement of experts, or a repeat founder applying a familiar approach.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Means-driven processes', which concern ad hoc combination of resources at hand rather than standing routines. Do not use when the person stresses genuine unexpectedness in the encounter.

codes.label: Opportunity discovered by alertness
codes.definition: The opportunity is treated as pre-existing and found through the entrepreneur's alertness, observation, general opportunity-spotting ability or traits. It is then pursued. Some authors criticise this view in favour of opportunities enacted or created collectively.
codes.applies_when: The person attributes the discovery to being on the lookout, generally good at spotting opportunities, or alert to an existing market gap, which was then pursued with gathered resources.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Spontaneous recognition without search', which involves information arriving by chance and being recognised through specific prior knowledge rather than general alertness. Also confused with 'Foresight or insight rather than chance', which concerns specific anticipation.

codes.label: Spontaneous recognition without search
codes.definition: Information arrives by chance, for example through social contacts, and a person with relevant prior knowledge recognises an opportunity without having been engaged in any quest or search. Dew treats this as distinct from serendipity, which arises during an active pursuit.
codes.applies_when: Someone with relevant knowledge happens to receive information and sees an opportunity, while not pursuing any search or other goal at the time.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Opportunity discovered by alertness', which credits general alertness rather than chance information meeting specific prior knowledge. Do not use when the person was actively pursuing another goal when the chance event occurred.

codes.label: Pre-discovery
codes.definition: During search, a person stumbles on something that seems significant but lacks the knowledge to evaluate it. Its value is realised only later, once complementary knowledge exists.
codes.applies_when: The account describes coming across something during work that seemed important but could not be understood or commercialised until much later.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Spontaneous recognition without search': there the person's prior knowledge allowed immediate recognition and there was no search. Do not use if existing knowledge let them see the implications at once.

codes.label: Innate genius or heroic personality
codes.definition: Discoveries or success are explained solely by the founder's innate gift, genius, knack or heroic, never-say-die character. Authors criticise this as tautological and as sidestepping specific reasoning practices.
codes.applies_when: The account credits the outcome only to the founder's natural talent, exceptional character or being the right kind of person.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Effort and persistence over luck', which credits sustained work rather than inborn traits. Do not use when the account describes specific recognition practices or the circumstances that produced the event.

codes.label: Effort and persistence over luck
codes.definition: Outcomes are explained by hard work, tenacity, will power, persistence, skill or relationships, explicitly rather than by luck or serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The person or a narrator attributes the result mainly to persistent effort, determination or seizing an opportunity others let pass, treating luck as minor.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Innate genius or heroic personality', which credits fixed traits rather than effort. Do not use if an unexpected find played a central role in the result.

codes.label: Impulsive personal drivers
codes.definition: Venturing steps are explained by impulse, disinhibition or personal disposition, which are internal dynamics that drive unreasoned action, rather than by an unexpected external event.
codes.applies_when: The account attributes an unplanned venturing step to the person's impulsivity, disinhibition or temperament.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Pure luck without agency': use that code when the unplanned element is an external chance event or encounter rather than the person's own impulses.

codes.label: Inevitability or obviousness
codes.definition: A seemingly serendipitous discovery is explained as obvious, in the air, or bound to happen given existing knowledge, timing or system behaviour. Chance only affected who made the discovery or when.
codes.applies_when: The account suggests the opportunity was widely known or obvious, that someone would have found it anyway, that the time was simply ripe, or that the supposedly accidental event followed predictably from earlier interactions.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Environmentally imposed direction', which concerns outside forces dictating the venture's course rather than the discovery being bound to happen. Do not use when the event was genuinely unforeseeable given existing knowledge.

codes.label: Environmentally imposed direction
codes.definition: The venture's emergence or direction is explained by market forces, institutions, reward structures, situational factors or general changes in circumstances that determine or force action, rather than by chance or choice.
codes.applies_when: The account says market imperatives, government, clients, institutional incentives, industry structure, selection forces or broad conditions such as access to finance or a poor economy dictated or triggered the venture's course, leaving little choice.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Acting on others' prompting or pressure', which concerns specific outside parties pointing out or pushing particular unexpected information. Also confused with 'Inevitability or obviousness'.

codes.label: Acting on others' prompting or pressure
codes.definition: The organisation acts on information mainly because others pointed it out and many followed, or because outside parties such as policymakers evaluated it and pressured the organisation to act.
codes.applies_when: The account shows the opportunity was suggested by others and pursued by many actors at once, or that the person acted on unexpected information because government or other outsiders pushed them to.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Environmentally imposed direction', which concerns broad structural forces rather than specific parties prompting action on particular information. Do not use when the person noticed and evaluated the information independently.

codes.label: Deliberate targeted networking
codes.definition: Valuable ties are explained as planned: the entrepreneur knew in advance which contacts or resources were needed and pursued them, or used referrals and intermediaries such as investors, rather than meeting people by chance.
codes.applies_when: The entrepreneur describes identifying a needed contact in advance and pursuing them, cold outreach, asking for referrals, negotiating with several partners in parallel, an investor introducing a cofounder, or leveraging existing acquaintances for a predefined goal.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Prior ties and network structure', which attributes outcomes to existing ties or similarity without deliberate goal-directed outreach. Do not use when the value of the connection was unknown beforehand.

codes.label: Prior ties and network structure
codes.definition: Outcomes or partnerships are explained by pre-existing relationships, network position, a preference for similar others, or the commitment of close contacts, rather than by unexpected encounters.
codes.applies_when: The account attributes the opportunity or collaboration to existing ties, network position, a close friend or family member's help, or seeking out similar others.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate targeted networking', which involves planned outreach for a known goal. Do not use when a new, unexpected meeting is central.

codes.label: Success credited to skill that chance could explain
codes.definition: Outcomes are attributed to skill, strategy or customer orientation when chance events, survivor-only evidence or alternative causes could equally explain them.
codes.applies_when: The account draws lessons about success from successful cases alone, infers that success proves good strategy or meeting customer needs, or credits skill while ignoring evident chance events or causes such as competitor weakness or shortages.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Reconstructed or embellished accident narrative', where the chance story itself is what has been constructed after the fact. Do not use when the person describes actively noticing and acting on an unexpected event.

codes.label: Reconstructed or embellished accident narrative
codes.definition: The story of an unplanned or lucky discovery may have been rationalised after the fact, exaggerated or second-hand, or luck may be invoked as a catch-all for otherwise unexplained outcomes.
codes.applies_when: There are signs that the accident narrative was reconstructed later, embellished relative to evidence of effort, or that luck or serendipity is cited loosely to explain what is otherwise unexplained.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Success credited to skill that chance could explain', which concerns skill stories that hide chance rather than chance stories that may hide effort.

codes.label: Need-pull or technology-push development
codes.definition: The venture or invention is explained as a planned response to an existing market need, or as pushing a technology or scientific discovery toward a use identified in advance, including through institutional incentives.
codes.applies_when: The account presents the idea as answering a known demand, as commercialising a technology toward a predefined use, or as steered by subsidies or technology-transfer programmes.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate systematic search': here the driver is a known need or technology capability rather than a search process. Do not use when the use emerged unanticipated.

codes.label: Founder created the enabling change
codes.definition: The external condition that enabled the venture was brought about by the founder, for example through their own invention or lobbying, rather than happening to them.
codes.applies_when: The account shows that the enabling technology, regulation or market change was produced by the founder's own actions.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Environmentally imposed direction', where the change arose independently of the actor and shaped the venture from outside.

codes.label: Imitative entry without trigger
codes.definition: Some ventures, notably me-too entries in mature industries, start without any identifiable external event or unexpected trigger.
codes.applies_when: The venture copies an existing business model in a stable industry, and the account names no distinct event behind its start.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Environmentally imposed direction', where a specific external change or condition prompted the start.

codes.label: Exploiting others' predictable misjudgments
codes.definition: Entrepreneurial profit or entry against incumbents is explained by deliberately exploiting others' systematic biases, as a non-random alternative to luck or serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The account explains success by recognising and exploiting what incumbents or others predictably misjudge or overlook.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Venture performance as random luck': use that code when the same success is attributed to chance.

codes.label: Engineered or algorithmic serendipity
codes.definition: Encounters that feel serendipitous were in fact produced by recommender systems, targeted ads or other people's arrangements. Critics hold that this is an illusion of serendipity rather than genuine chance.
codes.applies_when: The apparently chance encounter or find came through algorithmic recommendations, data-driven targeting or deliberate arrangement by someone else for their own ends.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Deliberate targeted networking', where the person themselves planned the encounter. Do not use when the encounter arose without targeting.

codes.label: Mere receipt of new information
codes.definition: Simply encountering new information, for example from a newsfeed or newsletter, is not serendipity if it brings no surprise, answers no felt question and prompts no follow-up.
codes.applies_when: The person merely learned a new fact, and it did not address a problem they had or prompt them to act.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Spontaneous recognition without search', where the chance information was recognised as an opportunity. Do not use when the information prompted surprise, investigation and use.

codes.label: Wishful 'something will turn up' optimism
codes.definition: Serendipity is invoked as shallow optimism, a belief that something will turn up that is used to avoid facing evident problems, rather than as an actual unsought discovery.
codes.applies_when: The account invokes luck or 'things will work out' while ignoring real problems, with no actual discovery described.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Pure luck without agency', which describes a fortunate event that actually happened rather than hoped-for luck.

codes.label: Zemblanity and suppressed serendipity
codes.definition: Zemblanity is the logical reverse of serendipity: actors unintentionally construct their own misfortune through ill-conceived choices, habits or settings. Bahramdipity is the suppression of serendipitous good outcomes, for example by hierarchical power.
codes.applies_when: The account frames an adverse surprise as bad luck but shows it arose from the actors' own choices, overconfidence, lax controls or habits, or describes a leader suppressing a promising unexpected opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Confused with 'Pure luck without agency', where the misfortune or fortune simply befell the person. Do not use for accidents caused purely by system complexity.

codes.label: Luck of place and timing
codes.definition: Being in a particular place at a particular moment, or small circumstantial differences, rather than superior ability, lead one person and not another to an opportunity. Sometimes several independent fortunate circumstances line up.
codes.applies_when: The person attributes the start or a turn of the venture to luck, timing, location or a coincidence of several fortunate circumstances rather than to their own attributes.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person credits their own alertness, curiosity or knowledge for spotting it. Code those under the individual trait or experience codes.

codes.label: High uncertainty and unclear goals
codes.definition: Serendipity matters most where outcomes cannot be known in advance, goals are emergent or ambiguous, the needed ties or resources are unknown, and the person has little control over the conditions of success.
codes.applies_when: The person says they could not foresee where actions would lead, did not know what the venture would become or whom they needed, and so acted on whatever came along.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account stresses rapid change in the market rather than not knowing; use the dynamic environment code.

codes.label: Dynamic, fast-changing environment
codes.definition: Rapidly changing or high-velocity markets, and information that arrives in stages, make unexpected discoveries more frequent and more valuable to pursue. One author dissents: incessant change can also undermine what was discovered before it pays off.
codes.applies_when: The person links an unexpected opportunity to fast or unpredictable change in their market or industry, a boom with a flow of new opportunities, or constantly arriving new information, or says constant change wiped out what they had noticed.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The emphasis is on not knowing outcomes or goals rather than on pace of change; use high uncertainty.

codes.label: Putting themselves in chance's way
codes.definition: The founder actively made unexpected opportunities more likely: going to events, talking to many people, trying many things, sharing their work.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes deliberate habits that invite chance. For example: 'I said yes to every coffee meeting that first year.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder only describes an attitude of being ready for chances, with no actions. Use "Ready to seize openings".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Setting the stage for chance. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Deliberately setting the stage for chance
draft_wording.definition: Serendipity cannot be planned, but people can raise its likelihood by actively putting themselves where chance is likely, positioning in the flow of opportunities and cultivating practices that make lucky finds more likely. Exposure alone gives no guarantee. One author holds that luck is uncontrollable and effort is better spent on becoming better informed.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes actively helping luck to happen, seeking out turbulent or opportunity-rich situations, varying routines or organising processes in anticipation of unexpected uses, rather than passively waiting. Also code when they say chance is beyond control and shift effort elsewhere.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The person describes a disposition of expecting luck rather than actions to create it; use expecting and welcoming serendipity.

codes.label: Expecting and welcoming serendipity
codes.definition: People who believe they are lucky, expect unexpected finds and have had positive past experiences of noticing become more open to serendipity and so luckier.
codes.applies_when: The person describes seeing themselves as lucky, treating unexpected finds as a normal part of their work, or says earlier noticing made them more attentive later.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person describes concrete actions to create chances; use deliberately setting the stage.

codes.label: Improvisation
codes.definition: The ability of a person or venture to react quickly, intentionally and creatively in the moment raises the chance of acknowledging and acting on unexpected events.
codes.applies_when: The person or venture improvised a fast creative response to an unexpected situation.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account is about loose rules or structure that permitted the response; use loose, flexible structure.

codes.label: Emotional state
codes.definition: Positive, especially other-oriented, emotions broaden attention and receptivity to triggers; negative emotions reduce it.
codes.applies_when: The person links their mood or emotional state to noticing or missing an unexpected opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account concerns a stable personality trait; use curiosity, openness and alertness.

codes.label: Sociable and reflective practices
codes.definition: Outgoing behaviour increases the number and diversity of encounters, while solitary practices such as reading, browsing or reflection help notice weak cues.
codes.applies_when: Frequent socialising or solitary reading, browsing, meditation or reflection preceded the unexpected input.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The focus is on the breadth or reach of the network rather than personal habits; use network breadth and weak ties.

codes.label: Active effort and search
codes.definition: Hard work, diligent and sustained activity, repeated exposure, habitual searching and entrepreneurial action such as networking and combining resources increase the number of chance encounters and finds.
codes.applies_when: The person links lucky opportunities to working hard, doing a lot, actively scanning, or regularly attending to a stream of information.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person stresses persisting after failure; use persistence through setbacks.

codes.label: Motivation and incentives to act
codes.definition: A prospect of profit, a personal need or frustration, a desire for self-employment, or the firm's existing interests shape whether a person notices and acts on an unexpected opportunity. Noticing without motivation does not lead to action.
codes.applies_when: The person explains noticing or acting, or not acting, by gain, dissatisfaction, wanting their own business, or how the opportunity fit existing business interests.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The issue is whether the opportunity was judged attractive or whether they felt capable; use judging whether to act.

codes.label: Judging whether to act
codes.definition: Whether an unexpected opportunity is pursued depends on a subjective, changing evaluation shaped by risk tolerance, timing, available information, and doubts that learning or encouragement can resolve.
codes.applies_when: The person describes weighing whether the unexpected idea was worth it, or overcoming doubt through learning or encouragement before acting.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The decision turned on low stakes; use low cost of trying.

codes.label: Effectual orientation
codes.definition: An effectual, means-driven way of thinking that embraces contingency, and a belief that one's actions can shape the environment, prepare the mind and lower the threshold for acting on the unexpected.
codes.applies_when: The person describes using surprises rather than avoiding them, starting from available means, or believing they can shape their surroundings.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account is specifically about capping losses; use low cost of trying.

codes.label: Cheap to try
codes.definition: Trying the new idea cost little, so the founder could act on the unexpected without much risk.
codes.applies_when: The founder says they could test it quickly and cheaply, or had a safety net. For example: 'It cost me $50 to see if anyone would buy it.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The point is lacking money to follow up. Use "Little money or resources".
codes.reason: Suggested core: Low cost of trying. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code

draft_wording.label: Low cost of trying
draft_wording.definition: When trying is cheap, failure affordable or a safety net exists, people stay open to accidents, run many small bets and act on unexpected opportunities; when failure is costly they avoid them.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person acted because little was at stake, used small fast trials or experiments within affordable loss, or avoided experiments because failure was expensive.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The point is having or lacking money to follow up a find; use time, money and support to follow up.

codes.label: Inexperience and outsider position
codes.definition: Being new to a field, an outsider to its norms and networks, or unaware of expert objections keeps people open and lets novel ideas survive. Authors differ: others see experience as enabling serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The person says being new, naive, an outsider or ignorant of conventional wisdom helped them spot or keep pursuing an unexpected idea.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person credits their experience or prior knowledge; use experience and prior knowledge.

codes.label: Expertise and functional fixedness
codes.definition: Growing mastery, specialisation and success in current activities narrow expectations, fix how tools and resources are seen and crowd out experimentation with new possibilities.
codes.applies_when: The person describes habitual uses, narrow specialisation, routine skill or commitment to core competence making them overlook or not follow up an unexpected option.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The dismissal stems from biases such as overconfidence or anchoring; use cognitive biases.

codes.label: Cognitive biases
codes.definition: Overconfidence, complacency, anchoring, illusion of control, underestimating the unexpected, self-censoring and denial lead people to dismiss or not search for unexpected information.
codes.applies_when: The person initially dismissed, doubted, denied or self-censored an unexpected finding, stopped searching from confidence, or stayed anchored to the original concept.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The blindness comes from specialist habits; use expertise and functional fixedness.

codes.label: No fixed plan
codes.definition: The founder held plans loosely, which left room to follow the unexpected; or held them rigidly, which nearly made them miss it.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes having no fixed plan and moving step by step. For example: 'We never had a business plan, so it was easy to switch.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: The limit came from obligations to investors or contracts. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Version 1.0 (25 Oct 2026): one idea per code; being locked into a plan goes to ANO-CND.

draft_wording.label: Rigid versus flexible plans
draft_wording.definition: Rigid adherence to detailed predefined plans or articulated strategies blinds people to unexpected opportunities; loose, general or incremental plans and emergent strategy leave room for them.
draft_wording.applies_when: The person describes holding plans loosely, proceeding step by step, or being locked into a plan that made them ignore an unexpected opportunity.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: The constraint comes from obligations to funders or sunk investments; use prior commitments.

codes.label: Broad versus narrow goals
codes.definition: Broad, aspirational or unspecified goals and loosely defined problems raise the chance of picking up the unexpected; narrow, over-specified goals, fixed criteria or task-focused productivity create selective inattention.
codes.applies_when: The person contrasts a broad mission or open-ended aim with tightly specified targets in relation to noticing or missing unexpected options.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account concerns where search was directed rather than how goals were set; use searching beyond the core.

codes.label: Searching beyond the core
codes.definition: Undirected, wide search and attention to peripheral users, markets, uses or domains outside one's usual focus increase unexpected discovery.
codes.applies_when: The person wandered into, looked at, or entered markets, users or fields far from their core, or kept the problem open while exploring broadly.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The point is goal breadth; use broad versus narrow goals.

codes.label: Too much openness and need for focus
codes.definition: Openness without focus leads to drifting between opportunities; some focus, simple screening rules and a balance of structure and chaos are needed. This qualifies the view that plans hinder serendipity.
codes.applies_when: The person describes chasing too many unexpected options, scattering resources, or using criteria to filter which surprises to pursue.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Planned work is credited with producing surprises; use planned work as a seedbed.

codes.label: Planned work as a seedbed
codes.definition: Serendipity arises within routine, goal-directed work and purposeful action, which also make surprises visible against the plan; alternating goal progress with open modes helps.
codes.applies_when: The surprise emerged while doing assigned, routine or planned tasks, or was noticed because it departed from a plan.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The person says plans blinded them; use rigid versus flexible plans.

codes.label: Prior commitments
codes.definition: Commitments to funders, contracts, assigned targets, sunk investments, dominant stories and accumulated stakeholder obligations limit the freedom to redirect toward unexpected opportunities.
