codes.applies_when: The person could not follow an unexpected lead because of investor expectations, contracted tasks, committed resources or earlier commitments.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The constraint is internal plan fixation; use rigid versus flexible plans.

codes.label: Formal control and efficiency drives
codes.definition: Stage-gates, Six Sigma, schedules, short-term metrics, bureaucratic top-down management and predefined innovation channels kill or ignore unexpected avenues. One author instead treats reliance on chance as a symptom of bureaucracy.
codes.applies_when: An unexpected opportunity was blocked, killed or ignored because of formal evaluation, schedules, efficiency pressure or a manager insisting on the plan.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account praises few rules and informal arrangements; use loose, flexible structure.

codes.label: Loose, flexible structure
codes.definition: Informal, flat and lightly structured organisations with simple rules and the ability to shift resources quickly can capture unexpected opportunities; heavy structure narrows them.
codes.applies_when: The account links informal arrangements, few rules or rapid redirection of resources to taking up an unexpected opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The focus is individual freedom to follow leads; use autonomy to follow leads.

codes.label: Autonomy to follow leads
codes.definition: Freedom from set assignments, decentralised decisions and permission for side initiatives let people pursue unexpected leads.
codes.applies_when: The person had freedom or discretion within an organisation to follow up an unexpected finding.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The freedom is specifically about time allocation; use slack time.

codes.label: Small size and concentrated authority
codes.definition: Small, young, owner-controlled ventures, and cases where the person doing the work also holds decision authority, can redirect quickly toward unexpected findings.
codes.applies_when: The person who spotted the opportunity could redirect resources directly, or adaptability is linked to the venture being small and owner-run.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Freedom is granted by a larger organisation; use autonomy to follow leads.

codes.label: Slack time
codes.definition: Discretionary time, unforced pace and informal downtime let people explore, notice and evaluate unexpected leads; rushing precludes them.
codes.applies_when: Free time, a slack rule, breaks or reserved exploration time allowed an unexpected discovery.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The room arose unplanned from a disruption to schedules; use unplanned latitude.

codes.label: Unplanned latitude
codes.definition: Unplanned moments that break schedule pressure give actors time to observe anomalies; the authors distinguish this from allocated slack.
codes.applies_when: Room or freedom from deadlines arose unexpectedly and let the person explore something.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The time was formally allocated; use slack time.

codes.label: Time, money and support to follow up
codes.definition: Financial cushion, prior investments, owners and resources determine whether a chance observation is pursued; collaboration costs can stall it. Authors differ from those who see scarcity as helpful.
codes.applies_when: Having or lacking money, time, an owner or support decided whether a chance find was pursued.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Scarcity is credited with prompting the discovery; use resource scarcity.

codes.label: Little money or resources
codes.definition: Having little money or few resources pushed the founder to rely on what turned up and improvise.
codes.applies_when: Being short of money or resources led the founder to improvise or take an unexpected opportunity. For example: 'We couldn't afford ads, so we said yes to any partnership.'
codes.does_not_apply_when: Lack of money stopped them following up. Leave this code off.
codes.reason: Suggested core: Resource scarcity; relevant to small ventures. Revised: plain wording for founder interviews, with a made-up example; meaning kept; neighbours named by core-code ID or misfit code | Shortened to the word limit (21 Oct). Code it when was: 'The founder says being short of money or resources led them to an unconventional solution or to take an unexpected opportunity.'

draft_wording.label: Resource scarcity
draft_wording.definition: Limited resources push small and early ventures to rely on what turns up and to improvise new uses for existing means. Authors differ from those who see resources as necessary.
draft_wording.applies_when: Lack of money or infrastructure made the venture rely on chance or led to an unconventional solution.
draft_wording.does_not_apply_when: Lack of resources stopped follow-up; use time, money and support to follow up.

codes.label: Unequal access
codes.definition: Serendipity is unequally distributed: privilege, networks and in-person presence widen access, while poverty, financial strain and marginal position sap attention and limit it.
codes.applies_when: The person notes that social position, financial pressure or lack of in-person contact limited or enabled chance encounters.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The issue is only the venture's own funds; use time, money and support.

codes.label: Attention load and multitasking
codes.definition: Attention is limited; authors differ on multitasking, some seeing broad simultaneous tasks as favourable, others finding overload or sequential work matters.
codes.applies_when: The person links juggling tasks, overload or one-at-a-time working to noticing or missing opportunities.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The account is about time slack; use slack time.

codes.label: Timing and fleeting windows
codes.definition: Events become valuable when they match the venture's current needs; opportunities must be acted on before limited windows close.
codes.applies_when: The person stresses the event came at the right stage or had to be seized quickly.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Timing is purely luck; use luck of place and timing.

codes.label: Retaining past knowledge
codes.definition: Storing and retrieving past ideas, failures and competences lets later chance connections occur.
codes.applies_when: A shelved idea, retained team or stored knowledge enabled a later discovery.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The stress is on long development time; use patience.

codes.label: Patience and long horizons
codes.definition: Serendipity needs long incubation; short investor horizons hinder it.
codes.applies_when: The account stresses years of engagement or timeline mismatch as obstacle.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use retaining past knowledge for revived stored ideas.

codes.label: Support for emerging ideas
codes.definition: Funding, evaluation, introductions and institutional support help turn unexpected ideas into ventures; perceived unfundability holds them back.
codes.applies_when: An investor, program or institution evaluated, funded or enabled an unexpected idea, or the person didn't seek funding expecting rejection.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use incubators and events when the setting created the encounter.

codes.label: Supportive leaders and champions
codes.definition: Leaders who invite anomalies, give permission, understand the domain, moderate settings, and champions who push ideas enable serendipity.
codes.applies_when: A leader, facilitator or champion encouraged, backed or made room for an unexpected direction.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Leaders suppress ideas; use power and hierarchy.

codes.label: Power and hierarchy
codes.definition: Politics, toxic leadership, status hierarchies and isolation from decision-makers suppress unexpected ideas.
codes.applies_when: An unexpected idea was blocked or ignored due to power, status or lack of access.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Blocking stems from formal processes; use formal control.

codes.label: Psychological safety and failure tolerance
codes.definition: Safety to speak up and tolerance of mistakes make people share and pursue unexpected ideas.
codes.applies_when: People felt safe or unsafe to raise odd ideas or risk failure.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use help-seeking norms for cooperation culture.

codes.label: Culture open to the unexpected
codes.definition: Cultures that legitimise unexpected ideas, tolerate messiness and encourage trying new things.
codes.applies_when: The account credits an organisational mindset of openness.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use psychological safety when fear of blame is central.

codes.label: Help-seeking and cooperative norms
codes.definition: Norms of asking for and giving help, cooperation and legitimacy of contacting strangers.
codes.applies_when: Culture of sharing or reaching out surfaced a useful idea.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use open information flow for channels.

codes.label: Open information flow
codes.definition: Communication across groups, many receptors and voices from margins let surprises surface; silos and unawareness hinder.
codes.applies_when: Information channels or silos shaped spotting opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use power and hierarchy for suppression.

codes.label: Mixing problems and solutions
codes.definition: Loose settings and brokering routines let problems meet solutions by chance.
codes.applies_when: An available solution met a problem through mixing people or units.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use diversity code for people differences.

codes.label: Codified knowledge reduces surprise
codes.definition: Well-catalogued, systematised knowledge yields fewer surprises; poorly catalogued niches yield more.
codes.applies_when: Formal repositories versus informal discovery affect finds.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use formal control for gates.

codes.label: Controlled sloppiness
codes.definition: Loose, untidy work with traceable loose ends lets unexpected results arise.
codes.applies_when: Person kept loose ends or variation that yielded finds.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use loose structure for organisational design.

codes.label: Diversity of people
codes.definition: Diverse, cross-boundary teams and interactions increase serendipity; homogeneous groups and groupthink constrain it.
codes.applies_when: Mixing different backgrounds produced an unexpected opportunity.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use similarity balance for overlap level.

codes.label: Balance of similarity
codes.definition: Encounters work best with some shared knowledge; authors differ on similar versus moderate overlap; too much overlap breeds rivalry.
codes.applies_when: Partner similarity or mix of familiar and new shaped outcome.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use diversity of people for general variety.

codes.label: Network breadth and weak ties
codes.definition: Broad networks and ties to strangers bring novel information; low proactive networking leaves reliance on chance ties.
codes.applies_when: Outreach beyond close circle or closed circle shaped encounters.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use designed spaces for physical settings.

codes.label: Exposure to many users and contexts
codes.definition: Exposing products to many users and contexts reveals new uses.
codes.applies_when: Users or other fields revealed new uses.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use searching beyond the core for founder exploration.

codes.label: Designed spaces and proximity
codes.definition: Shared spaces, proximity and matching practices raise chance encounters; co-location alone may not suffice.
codes.applies_when: Shared space or random pairing caused an encounter.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use incubators and events for programs.

codes.label: Incubators, events and browsing venues
codes.definition: Incubators, fairs, conferences and browsing venues expose people to unplanned connections.
codes.applies_when: Chance encounter occurred at such a venue.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use designed spaces for layout.

codes.label: Dense knowledge-rich setting
codes.definition: Dense clusters and communities raise serendipity.
codes.applies_when: Encounter placed in a dense hub.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use incubators for programs.

codes.label: Nascent or frontier field
codes.definition: Early, empirical, frontier fields and immature technologies yield more accidents.
codes.applies_when: Person links chance finds to new field.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use broadly applicable technology for generic tech.

codes.label: Broadly applicable technology
codes.definition: Technologies with wide potential application ease transfer to unexpected uses.
codes.applies_when: Generic technology transferred to new field.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use nascent field for early-stage domains.

codes.label: Complex open-ended settings
codes.definition: Multi-actor, evolving projects and landscapes with many viable directions favour serendipity.
codes.applies_when: Rich project with many actors produced surprise.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use diversity for people variety.

codes.label: Strength and kind of event
codes.definition: Novel, disruptive events and qualitative facts are likelier to trigger serendipity.
codes.applies_when: Event described as jolting or qualitatively novel.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use luck code for coincidences.

codes.label: Guiding theory of value
codes.definition: A distinctive vision or understanding of direction helps recognise unexpected value.
codes.applies_when: Vision helped frame a surprise as valuable.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use broad goals for goal breadth.

codes.label: Refusing received conventions
codes.definition: Refusing norms, standards and paradigms enables novel uses.
codes.applies_when: Person defied conventions about resources or norms.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use generative doubt for own assumptions.

codes.label: Noisy feedback keeps options alive
codes.definition: Imprecise feedback and loosely connected networks let discarded options survive.
codes.applies_when: Option survived via inertia or small group.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use persistence for deliberate tenacity.

codes.label: Self-reinforcing dynamics amplify chance
codes.definition: Retained gains and network effects magnify chance events.
codes.applies_when: Early lucky gain kept paying off.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use shocks code for erased advantage.

codes.label: Shocks erasing chance advantage
codes.definition: Environmental shifts nullify accumulated advantages.
codes.applies_when: Shift made earlier advantages useless.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use amplification code when gains persist.

codes.label: Reputation for quality
codes.definition: Commitment to quality and clients opens chance opportunities.
codes.applies_when: Opportunity credited to reputation.
codes.does_not_apply_when: Use network breadth for contacts.

codes.label: Abstracting the idea to its core
codes.definition: Founders respond to criticism by moving the idea to a more abstract level so that the core survives while details change.
codes.applies_when: The founder restates the idea at a higher level (the purpose or need) after criticism of specifics.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Visionary versus scientist self-image
codes.definition: Founders narrate themselves either as visionaries who hold to the idea or as scientists who test it.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes their stance toward the idea as visionary conviction or as experimental testing.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Idea described as sparked or born
codes.definition: Founders describe the origin of their idea as a spark or birth, a sudden moment rather than a search.
codes.applies_when: The founder narrates the idea as sparked, born or arriving at a moment.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Board resists tangents
codes.definition: Investors or board members discourage the founders from following side opportunities, even surprising ones.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes investors or a board pushing back on following an unexpected opportunity.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Enjoyment of the activity
codes.definition: Users who enjoy the activity are more likely to keep innovating and to drift into founding.
codes.applies_when: The founder says they did it because they loved the activity or hobby.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Small niche market
codes.definition: User entrepreneurship is more likely in niche markets that established firms ignore.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes a small or specialised market large firms did not serve.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Unstable setting enables emergence
codes.definition: Decline, new leadership, a struggle over identity and ongoing conflict push an organisation away from stability, making it more likely that a small change emerges and is amplified.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes a period of crisis, turmoil or searching just before the unplanned change.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Negative feedback limits the change
codes.definition: Complaints and resistance check the amplifying cycle and limit how far and fast change goes.
codes.applies_when: The founder describes pushback from neighbours, members or authorities that slowed or reshaped the change.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Change described as organic
codes.definition: People describe the change as organic, as something that just grew, rather than as planned.
codes.applies_when: The founder says the venture or change 'just grew' or was 'organic'.
codes.reason: New: from the six papers read on 21 Oct 2026 (harness/codebook/added_papers.json).

codes.label: Credited to their own effort
codes.definition: The founder credits the outcome to their own effort, persistence or work, whether or not they set it against luck.
codes.applies_when: The founder says success came from persisting, working hard, staying in the field or listening. For example (Brownell et al. 2024, p. 1711): founders said 'their success occurred because they were able to persist despite earlier setbacks'.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder splits credit between luck and effort. Use "Part luck, part effort".
The founder credits luck alone. Use "Credited to luck".
codes.change_note: Round 2: four founders credit persistence, work or listening without contrasting it with luck, which the code required. Brownell et al. (2024, p. 1711) find this perseverance theme; Baron (1998) states that entrepreneurs see their own effort as crucial. Extended rather than a new code, which would nearly duplicate it.

absorbs.comment: The founder credits staying in the field long enough for openings to come.
The founder credits his steady work, set against effortless viral success rather than luck.
The founder credits listening to customers, staff and suppliers.
The founder credits success in proportion to the work put in.

codes.label: Set the venture back
codes.definition: A chance event hurt or threatened the venture without starting, redirecting or advancing it.
codes.applies_when: The founder tells an unexpected event that cost the venture customers, money or time, or nearly ended it, and no new direction came from it. For example (Brownell et al. 2024, p. 1711): their data suggest 'that bad luck can prevent new venture success'.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The event also started the venture. Use "Started the venture".
The event also changed what the venture does. Use "Changed the venture's direction".
The setback is only background, with no effect told. Leave this code off.
codes.change_note: Round 2: two cases where a chance event only harmed the venture, and no role code fit. Brownell et al. (2024, p. 1711), read in full, state that bad luck can prevent venture success. Liu and Tsay (2023) and Liu and de Rond (2016) only lean on it.

absorbs.comment: COVID took the business to zero and nearly ended it; nothing new came of it.
A death in the founder's family caused a sales slump; it only hurt the venture.

codes.label: Built on an existing firm
codes.definition: The venture was built inside an established firm, or with that firm's time, money, staff or customers.
codes.applies_when: The founder pursued the find from within another firm they worked in or owned, using its resources. For example (Garud et al. 2011, p. 757): 3M's time option let employees 'leverage serendipitous moments … whenever they occurred'.
codes.does_not_apply_when: The founder only carried knowledge or contacts from an earlier job. Use "Idea grew from their work" or "Their network brought it".
codes.change_note: Round 2: two cases built on an existing firm's resources. Garud et al. (2011), read in full, make it central: 3M staff pursue chance finds with company time and resources. Buenstorf (2007) and Busch and Grimes (2023) only lean on it.

absorbs.comment: The founder used his existing software company's staff and contacts to act on the find.
The brand was built inside an established retail chain, answering customer demand.

codes.label: Proof of demand
codes.definition: The chance event showed the founder that people wanted the offering, before or without sales.
codes.applies_when: Offers, requests or eager uptake by others told the founder there was demand, even if no sale followed. For example (Shah and Tripsas 2007, p. 130): user-innovators 'received unsolicited requests from others wishing to purchase their innovations'.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
Sales or measured growth followed. Use "Growth and results".
It showed a new group of customers or a new use. Use "A new market or opportunity".
codes.change_note: Round 2: one case of declined offers taken as proof of demand, part of the theme 'results no outcome code names', which is split. Shah and Tripsas (2007, pp. 130-132), read in full, state it. The theme's other parts stay open.

absorbs.comment: Unsought offers to buy were declined but taken as proof of demand.

codes.label: Ready to seize openings
codes.definition: The founder describes an attitude of being ready to take unexpected openings, even when they feel risky.
codes.applies_when: The founder says they say yes to chances or are always ready to be surprised, without describing actions that bring chance their way. For example (Kirzner 1997, p. 72): 'An entrepreneurial attitude is one which is always ready to be surprised'.
codes.does_not_apply_when:
The founder describes actions that bring chance their way. Use "Putting themselves in chance's way".
The founder only says they believe in luck. Leave this code off.
codes.change_note: Round 2: one case of a stated readiness to take scary openings. Kirzner (1997, p. 72) and Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017, p. 192), read in full, state readiness as an attitude, kept apart from actions that raise exposure to chance.

absorbs.comment: The founder advises taking openings even when they feel scary: an attitude, not described habits.
